- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

# Todo

This file uses [Prose form](AGENTS.md#prose-form). It
contains near term tasks with a short description and
uses links or reference links for more details.

## In Progress

When a `## Todo` item is picked up, its text moves here: the
problem overview and its list of things to do. That is followed
by the "plan" — a bulleted list of the development "ladder":
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-0 blah (done)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-1 blah blah (current)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-2 blah blah blah
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y close-out and validation

**feat: grade the run from raw batches**

The 0.23.0 cycle, decided in
[Replanning II](notes/chores/chores-04.md#replanning-ii-drop-the-adjustment-grade-the-run):
the overhead subtraction estimates an ill-defined quantity and
cancels in same-harness A/B anyway, while the calibration-time
grade certified the room, not the exam. Drop the adjustment
machinery; grade the run from its own time-ordered batches.

- [[67]] 0.23.0-0 `chore: open raw-batch grading cycle`
  (done)
- [[68]] 0.23.0-1 `feat: micro-probe inner-loop sizing`
  (done) —
  `pick_inner` inputs from a ~1 ms micro-probe (low quantile
  over back-to-back timer pairs), never printed; unhooks
  sizing from `cfg.overhead`
- [[N]] 0.23.0-2 `feat: time-ordered batch pipeline`
  (done) —
  samples land in a raw batch buffer; per-batch summaries
  (floor, mean, census counts) taken as batches fill, then
  bulk-record into the histogram; bounded memory
- [[N]] 0.23.0-3 `feat: batch-based run gauge` (done) — relocate
  the -6 grade machinery (signals, thresholds, letter) onto
  batch summaries: drift from floor movement, bursts localized
  in time, interference rate from census counts (absorbs the
  crossover entry's rate analysis); print each signal's own
  letter beside its value (the scores already exist — the
  composite is their worst, and showing them makes every letter
  self-explaining). Lands while calibrate still exists, so the
  two grades can be sanity-checked against each other
  - **reports, never warns** (decided 2026-07-28): the report's
    job is a histogram faithful to what was measured, and a
    run's steadiness is largely the workload's character — a
    blocking round-trip is genuinely less steady than a
    spinning one. The letter is that fact, not a fault
- [[N]] 0.23.0-4 `feat: environment grade from warmup` —
  the box's own grade, measured before the workload's
  character enters the numbers: repeat the -1 micro-probe
  during warmup and grade its spread / movement. Separate
  signals and letter from the run grade; both print. Warmup
  is the only workload-independent window, so this is the
  environment certificate that must exist before -6 deletes
  `calibrate` (build-then-demolish). Coordinate with the
  "Dynamic startup warmup" Todo, which rewrites the same

111	     step-cost sizing pass, repeated back to back until K
112	     consecutive floors agree within tolerance; the final
113	     agreeing floor is the sizing input, so sizing is
114	     post-ramp by construction and convergence is tested on
115	     the number actually consumed (the micro-probe supplies
116	     the frame input, run after convergence)
117	   - K defaults to 3: two agreeing passes can certify a dwell
118	     at an intermediate P-state (the staircase ramp), not the
119	     top

122	     repetition climbs it into a fast state (~0.445 ns/iter,
123	     drift bracket caught 48.6 -> 45.3 mid-window, D/F),
124	     low-duty isolated runs sit at ~0.489 (B), ~9% apart, and
125	     transitions straddle windows in *both* directions (the
126	     climb under quick cadence; the settle-back after load,
127	     which outlasted an 8 s gap once the box had been hot);
128	     fixed warmup absorbs only transitions shorter than
129	     itself, whatever their sign
130	   - floors, not means, so one preemption doesn't fake
131	     (in)stability; warm box exits near-immediately
132	   - slow steps (`inner` -> 1 territory): pass length adapts
133	     — minimum step count or minimum wall time, whichever is
134	     larger — so a floor is never one sample; the cap exit
135	     then distinguishes "floors disagreed" (unstable, gauge
136	     signal) from "too slow to certify K passes" (proceed,
137	     label the run uncertified — at `inner = 1` sizing can't
138	     be wrong and framing is negligible, so the stakes are

# iiac-perf

A general-purpose latency microbenchmark harness for Rust. Each
bench runs against a wall-clock time budget with auto-sized loop
counts, reports a percentile-band histogram in nanoseconds, and
subtracts calibrated apparatus overhead (the amortized
loop-per-iter cost plus the dither-measured in-interval slice of
the timer pair; the full call-to-call timer cost instead sizes
the inner loop) so the output reflects the workload, not the
measurement loop.

Highlights:

- Time-based runs (`-d SECONDS` per bench, `-D SECONDS` total)
  with auto-sized outer/inner loop counts.
- Band-based histogram (min→p1, p1→p10, …, p99→max) with count,
  mean, range, and an adjusted-mean column.
- Per-thread CPU pinning (`--pin`) with independent calibration
  pinning (`--no-pin-cal`), so the cal environment stays stable
  regardless of where bench threads land.
- Plug in new workloads by implementing the `Bench` trait and
  registering in `src/benches/`.

The first benches measure Inter-Intra Application Communication
— function calls, async calls, channels, serde — which is what
seeded the project name. The harness itself is workload-agnostic.
The `ice-*` benches measure iceoryx2 shared-memory IPC inside one
process, in both of its messaging patterns (`ice-ps-*`
publish/subscribe, `ice-rr-*` request/response) at one and two
threads.

## Design (0.2.0)

Design a Rust app that can measure the cost of various (IIAC) techniques.
By IIAC I mean all communication techniques between and within
applications such as regular function calls vs async function calls vs
channels vs serde/deser of json or zero-copy messaging using io_uring and
potentially any other technique. It would include between threads or
processes or apps on the same computer or between apps on the same LAN or
between apps over a WAN.

Ideally I'd like to be able to see a histogram of the range of times of the
send and receive costs, not just the mean/average of 10^3 or 10^6 invocations.
So the cost of the work should or could be something near-zero such as just
echoing the input, but maybe there is value in doing some constant but
variable amount of work to verify it's in-consequential. One thing I think we
need to be aware of is that if we make the work too simple the compiler could
just keep things in registers which would not be representative of "real" work.

We should start simple, like comparing normal and async function calls and
later expand to other techniques.

## Usage

```
iiac-perf [BENCH...] [-d SECONDS] [-o OUTER] [-i INNER]
iiac-perf calibrate
iiac-perf add-completion-yaml
```

`BENCH` is one or more registered bench names, or `all` for every
registered bench. A name that matches no bench exactly runs every
bench it is a prefix of — `ice` runs all iceoryx2 benches, `mpsc`
runs `mpsc-1t` and `mpsc-2t`. **With no arguments, `iiac-perf` prints the
available list and exits — that's the source of truth for which
benches the current build registers.**

`iiac-perf calibrate` runs the startup calibration only — no
bench — and prints the
[Calibration banner](#calibration-banner) plus the raw fit
inputs: the dithered points, the three alternative fits, the
TSC tick rate, and the calibration wall time. Use it to
fingerprint a machine's frequency regime or check constant
drift without spending a bench run. The word must stand alone
(no bench names alongside); `--pin`, `--no-pin-cal`, and `-v`
apply as usual.

`iiac-perf add-completion-yaml` (also stand-alone) installs the
carapace completion spec: Tab then completes bench names, command
words, and flags in any carapace-served shell — without it,

# Claude in Chrome browser automation

You have access to browser automation tools (mcp__claude-in-chrome__*) for interacting with web pages in Chrome. Follow these guidelines for effective browser automation.

## Loading deferred tools

If the mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load every tool you expect to need in ONE ToolSearch call — the select query accepts a comma-separated list — never one call per tool. Start with the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting.

## GIF recording

When performing multi-step browser interactions that the user may want to review or share, use mcp__claude-in-chrome__gif_creator to record them.

You must ALWAYS:
* Capture extra frames before and after taking actions to ensure smooth playback
* Name the file meaningfully to help the user identify it later (e.g., "login_process.gif")

## Console log debugging

You can use mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages to read console output. Console output may be verbose. If you are looking for specific log entries, use the 'pattern' parameter with a regex-compatible pattern. This filters results efficiently and avoids overwhelming output. For example, use pattern: "[MyApp]" to filter for application-specific logs rather than reading all console output.

## Alerts and dialogs

IMPORTANT: Do not trigger JavaScript alerts, confirms, prompts, or browser modal dialogs through your actions. These browser dialogs block all further browser events and will prevent the extension from receiving any subsequent commands. Instead, when possible, use console.log for debugging and then use the mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages tool to read those log messages. If a page has dialog-triggering elements:
1. Avoid clicking buttons or links that may trigger alerts (e.g., "Delete" buttons with confirmation dialogs)
2. If you must interact with such elements, warn the user first that this may interrupt the session
3. Use mcp__claude-in-chrome__javascript_tool to check for and dismiss any existing dialogs before proceeding

If you accidentally trigger a dialog and lose responsiveness, inform the user they need to manually dismiss it in the browser.

## Avoid rabbit holes and loops

When using browser automation tools, stay focused on the specific task. If you encounter any of the following, stop and ask the user for guidance:
- Unexpected complexity or tangential browser exploration
- Browser tool calls failing or returning errors after 2-3 attempts
- No response from the browser extension
- Page elements not responding to clicks or input
- Pages not loading or timing out
- Unable to complete the browser task despite multiple approaches

Explain what you attempted, what went wrong, and ask how the user would like to proceed. Do not keep retrying the same failing browser action or explore unrelated pages without checking in first.

## Tab context and session startup

IMPORTANT: At the start of each browser automation session, call mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp first to get information about the user's current browser tabs. Use this context to understand what the user might want to work with before creating new tabs.

Never reuse tab IDs from a previous/other session. Follow these guidelines:
1. Only reuse an existing tab if the user explicitly asks to work with it
2. Otherwise, create a new tab with mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp
3. If a tool returns an error indicating the tab doesn't exist or is invalid, call tabs_context_mcp to get fresh tab IDs
4. When a tab is closed by the user or a navigation error occurs, call tabs_context_mcp to see what tabs are available

The wait-policy split dominates the 2-thread rows: the parking
benches (`mpsc-2t` and the probe family, all blocking `recv`)
cluster at ~7.4-8.1 µs while the spinning benches sit under
1.2 µs. For context, iceoryx2's own pub/sub benchmark (v0.9.2,

Here is the convo, arduously copy/pasted, link to an extension I can use in the future. Also note, I have 3 Pimoroni Pico Plus 2 right in front of me:

Q1:
I'm thinking of a high performance SPSC where the buffer is cache aligned thus there are always unused lower bits in the "address" (either direct address or a byte offset). Can we use bit 0 as a full empty flag so there is no need a separate shared counter/index to the next free/last filled?

A1:
Yes — and you've essentially re-derived the FastForward queue design (Giacomoni et al., PPoPP '08), which is a good sign because it's one of the fastest known SPSC structures. The key move is exactly what you're describing: put the full/empty state *in the slot itself*, and then you need no shared head/tail at all. Producer and consumer each keep a purely private local index that they increment modulo N. Producer: load slot with acquire, if "empty" then store `payload | 1` with release. Consumer: load with acquire, if bit 0 set, take payload, store "empty" (0) with release. No shared counters, no RMW instructions anywhere, no wasted slot to disambiguate full-vs-empty at wraparound, and full N capacity usable.

The tag bit specifically earns its keep in your shared-memory case. With process-local pointers you can just use NULL as the empty sentinel and skip the bit. But for shm you'll be storing byte offsets into the segment, and offset 0 can be a valid location — so `offset | 1` = full, `0` = empty is clean, and your cache-aligned message pool guarantees the low 6 bits are free. It also composes nicely with your pre-allocated pool model: the slot word is the entire message handoff (zero-copy, pointer/offset is the payload), and a single 8-byte release store publishes both the data and the flag atomically, so there's no separate "write payload then write flag" ordering to manage. On x86 that's just a plain `mov` each way.

Two caveats worth knowing before you benchmark it against zcr-mpsc in iiac-perf:

The first is the failure mode if you were instead thinking of tagging a *shared* index word (one word holding "next free/last filled" plus a flag). Don't — that makes both threads write the same cache line and forces CAS/exchange, which throws away the whole single-writer-per-line advantage of SPSC. The per-slot-flag version is the right reading of your idea.

The second is real, though: in the latency-critical near-empty regime (which is your steady state for an actor runtime), producer and consumer are always operating on the *same slot's* cache line, so every message costs a full coherence round trip — producer's store invalidates consumer's copy, consumer's read pulls it Shared, consumer's writeback invalidates producer's copy again. That's two-ish line transfers per message. The index-based design with cached indices (Rigtorp-style, where each side caches the other's index and only re-reads on apparent full/empty) has the same problem near-empty but amortizes beautifully under throughput load. FastForward's answer was "temporal slipping" — deliberately keeping the consumer a few slots behind — which buys throughput at the cost of latency, probably the wrong trade for you. In practice on a single Zen 2 CCX the ping-pong is ~40ish ns through L3, and the flag design still tends to win or tie at low occupancy because it touches exactly one line per message versus three (slot + two index lines) for the naive two-index version.

One micro-refinement to consider measuring: since the consumer's writeback of `0` is one of the two coherence transfers, there's a variant where the consumer doesn't clear the slot and instead a per-lap parity bit distinguishes stale from fresh (`offset | lap_bit`), making slots producer-write-only. The catch is the producer then can't tell from the slot whether it's been consumed, so the consumer has to publish its index occasionally anyway — you end up hybrid. Worth an HDR histogram side-by-side, but I'd expect the plain FastForward-with-tag-bit version to be the sweet spot for your round-trip benchmark.

Q2:
So on an X86-64 Intel or AMD can I assign the ISR to always run on a particular core and then assign the other end of the SPSC to be on that same core? If so there should be a decent chance that both sides will have a cache hit?

A2:
Yes, both halves are pinnable, and the payoff is better than "decent chance" — it changes the cache story qualitatively.

**Mechanics.** Thread side: `sched_setaffinity`/`pthread_setaffinity_np` to core X. IRQ side: write a mask to `/proc/irq/N/smp_affinity` (or `smp_affinity_list`) for that vector — MSI/MSI-X vectors are individually steerable, so a specific device interrupt can be nailed to core X. Two gotchas: kill or configure `irqbalance`, or it'll migrate the vector out from under you; and on modern kernels many drivers use threaded IRQs (or `force_irqthreads`), which splits the ISR into a tiny hard-irq top half plus a kernel thread (`irq/N-name`) — that thread has its own affinity you need to pin too, and it follows the hard-irq affinity by default but verify. If your "ISR" is actually user-space (UIO/VFIO with the eventfd reader, or your simulated one), it's just another thread pin.

**The cache consequence.** Same core means the slot's cache line never migrates. Producer store leaves it Modified in the local L1; consumer load hits it there; consumer's clear keeps it Modified in place. Zero coherence transactions, zero invalidations — the ~40 ns Zen 2 ping-pong we discussed simply doesn't exist. Both sides hit L1 essentially always, modulo the ISR handler's own code and data evicting some of the consumer's working set (L1 is 32 KB; a lean handler barely dents it, a fat driver path can).

**The memory model consequence, which is the fun part.** A single core observes its own stores in program order, and interrupts are precise — the ISR sees everything the interrupted thread did, and vice versa on return. So producer/consumer on one core is signal-handler semantics, not concurrency: you don't need *hardware* ordering at all, only compiler ordering. In Rust terms, keep the `Atomic*` types but every acquire/release could legally be `Relaxed`-plus-`compiler_fence` — and since x86 acquire/release loads/stores compile to plain `mov` anyway, just leave them as acquire/release and pay nothing. What you must never do on this layout is spin *inside the ISR* waiting on the consumer (drop-on-full only — the consumer cannot run while you're in the handler; you'd deadlock the core), but that was already your ISR constraint.

**The trade you're making.** You've eliminated coherence latency but serialized execution: the ISR now steals cycles from the consumer instead of running in parallel on another core, and the handoff latency becomes interrupt entry/exit plus scheduler-free resume — the consumer literally cannot observe the message until the ISR returns. For a spinning consumer that's excellent and very deterministic: interrupt fires, preempts the spin loop mid-`pause`, handler does one L1 store, `iret`, the very next slot load hits. Total added latency is the hardware interrupt path (~1–2 µs through the Linux hard-irq machinery, much less on bare metal/RTOS — this dwarfs any cache effect either way, which is worth internalizing: on Linux the interrupt path cost makes the same-core vs cross-core cache question mostly academic for real ISRs). Cross-core, by contrast, lets the handler and consumer overlap, which wins when the consumer does nontrivial per-message work at high rates.

**One config detail that matters more than the pinning:** keep that core in C0. If the consumer spins, fine. If it ever sleeps, an idle core in C6 adds tens of microseconds of wake latency to the interrupt — `cpuidle` limits (`cpu_dma_latency` / `idle=poll` on the isolated core) or the spinning consumer itself solves it. Combine with `isolcpus`/`nohz_full` on that core and you also stop the scheduler tick and other vectors from landing there, which is what actually cleans up the tail in your histograms.

So for the benchmark matrix this gives you a fifth configuration worth measuring: same-core (interrupt-preempt handoff, no coherence) vs same-CCX cross-core vs cross-CCX. My prediction: same-core wins on median and determinism for your steady-state timer case, cross-core same-CCX wins whenever consumer work per message exceeds roughly the coherence round trip, and the RP2350 version of this story (where "same core" means the M33 servicing the IRQ) will look like the bare-metal ideal of it.

Q3:
On Linux thread affinity does not mean that thread isn't used for anything else although that maybe a possibility?

A3:
Right — you've got the direction of the guarantee correct. Affinity constrains where *that thread* may run; it says nothing about what else runs on that core. By default core X still gets: other runnable user threads (the scheduler happily load-balances onto it), per-CPU kernel threads (`ksoftirqd/X`, `kworker/X:*`, `migration/X`, `rcu` machinery), the scheduler tick, timer callbacks, other IRQ vectors, and TLB-shootdown/function-call IPIs from the rest of the system. That's exactly the stuff that shows up as the fat tail in a latency histogram — a `kworker` deciding to flush something on your core is a multi-microsecond hole.

Making the core effectively exclusive is a stack of opt-outs, roughly in order of impact:

- **`isolcpus=X`** (or cpusets / `cset shield`, or systemd `CPUAffinity=` for everything else): removes the core from the general scheduler domain, so only explicitly-pinned threads land there. This is the "possibility" you're gesturing at — it exists but is opt-in at boot or via cgroup partitioning, not implied by affinity. The modern non-boot-param route is cgroup v2 `cpuset.cpus.partition=isolated`.
- **`nohz_full=X`**: stops the periodic scheduler tick on that core while it runs a single thread — removes the 100–1000 Hz timer interrupt that otherwise perforates your spin loop.
- **`rcu_nocbs=X`**: offloads RCU callbacks to threads you can pin elsewhere.
- **`irqaffinity=`** boot param plus per-vector `smp_affinity`: steer *default* IRQ placement away from the core, then pin only your device's vector to it.
- Residual `kworker`s: some per-CPU work can't be moved (writeback mostly can, via `/sys/bus/workqueue/devices/writeback/cpumask`), and `migration/X` and `ksoftirqd/X` will always exist but should be near-silent on an isolated tickless core.

What you can never exclude from userspace: SMIs (firmware-level, invisible to the kernel except via `turbostat`'s SMI counter — worth checking your board, some BIOSes fire them periodically for fan/EC polling) and, on the same-core-ISR layout from before, your own device's interrupt, which is of course the point.

Practical note for the benchmark: `isolcpus` + `nohz_full` + `rcu_nocbs` on two cores of one CCX gets you 99.99th percentiles that actually reflect the queue rather than the OS. And there's a diagnostic worth running once before trusting any numbers: pin a pure TSC-sampling spin loop on the isolated core and histogram the gaps between successive reads — any gap over ~a few hundred ns is an intrusion (tick, IRQ, SMI), and that "silence histogram" is your noise floor. If the noise floor isn't clean, no queue comparison on top of it is.

The RTOS/bare-metal contrast is basically why this matters for your flight-controller thinking: on the RP2350 you get core exclusivity by construction, and the Linux tuning above is an attempt to approximate that on a general-purpose kernel. `PREEMPT_RT` helps a different problem (bounded kernel preemption when you *do* take interrupts) but doesn't remove the intrusions — isolation does.

Q4:
Sooo I can construct an SPSC that uses bit 0 for used/available and even in the "poll" case it will have much better performance and narrower histogram and the long tail will be less dense. It may not be shorter, in the worse case, but fewer readings in the long tail?

A4:
Yes, that's the right summary — with one attribution worth keeping straight: the two properties come from different sources.

The **queue design** (slot flag, private indices, one cache line per message) is what buys the better median and the *narrowness* of the main lobe. The polling fast path is a single acquire load that either hits L1 (same-core or quiet slot) or costs one deterministic coherence transfer (cross-core). There's no shared-index line to contend on, no RMW whose latency varies with contention, no "re-read the other side's index" slow path that fires data-dependently. Fewer variable-latency operations per message = tighter distribution, almost by construction. A two-index design has more moving parts whose costs depend on occupancy history, which smears the distribution even when nothing external intrudes.

The **tail density vs. tail length** distinction is exactly right, and it's governed by the environment, not the queue. The worst-case reading is set by the worst intrusion — an SMI, a stray IPI, a thermal event — and no queue structure shortens that; if a 50 µs SMI lands between produce and consume, that sample is 50 µs regardless of how elegant the handoff is. What isolation (isolcpus/nohz_full/rcu_nocbs/IRQ steering) does is reduce the *rate* of intrusions, thinning the tail's population without necessarily lowering its maximum. And the queue design contributes a little here too, indirectly: fewer instructions and fewer cache lines per message means a smaller time window per handoff during which an intrusion can land *inside* the measurement, so marginally fewer samples get contaminated at all.

So the histogram you should expect: tall narrow mode at the L1-or-one-coherence-hop latency, a small deterministic shoulder (the "consumer just missed it and looped once" case), then a sparse scatter of environment-caused outliers whose *positions* are about the same as any other design's but whose *count* is low. The honest way to report it — and the useful iiac-perf output — is percentiles plus max as separate claims: p50/p99/p99.9 reflect your design, max reflects your platform. If someone (including future-you) compares queues by max alone on a non-isolated box, they're measuring the kernel, not the queue.

One falsifiable check to close the loop: run the same queue on isolated vs. non-isolated cores. Design effects should leave p50 nearly identical and mostly reshape p99.9+; if p50 moves a lot between those runs, something else is wrong (frequency scaling, C-states, wrong core pairing).

Q5:
On an RP2350 there are 4 cores 2 ARM, 2 RISC-V of which only 2 run at once, what are its cache coherence architecture?

A5;
Short answer: it doesn't have one, because it doesn't need one — there are no per-core data caches to keep coherent. This makes the RP2350 the degenerate (and pleasant) case of everything we've been discussing.

**The memory system.** Each core (whether you've booted the Cortex-M33s or the Hazard3 RISC-V cores — the selection is per-socket at boot, two running at once in any mix) talks straight to SRAM through a crossbar bus fabric. The 520 KB of SRAM is split into 10 banks: 8 large banks that are word-striped by default (consecutive words rotate across banks, spreading load), plus 2 small 4 KB direct-mapped banks intended as core-local scratch. Every access is uncached and single-cycle *when unarbitrated*. The only cache in the system is the XIP cache in front of QSPI flash — and since it sits in the fabric, both cores go *through the same cache*, so it's coherent by unification rather than by protocol. (The one sharp edge: if you write flash or use the XIP window in exotic ways, there are cache maintenance ops, but that's code, not your data path.)

**What replaces coherence traffic: arbitration.** Two masters (cores, plus DMA) hitting the *same bank* in the same cycle stall one of them for a cycle. That's the entire contention story — no MESI states, no invalidations, no line migration, no ping-pong. Your SPSC slot word being hammered by both cores costs at most occasional single-cycle arbitration stalls, deterministic and tiny. This is why the RP2350 histogram will look like the platonic ideal of your benchmark: the "coherence round trip" term is literally zero, and the tail intrusions are only interrupts you chose to enable.

**Ordering still matters architecturally, though.** No caches doesn't mean no memory model. The M33 is in-order and in practice doesn't reorder your stores, but ARMv8-M *permits* reordering to Normal memory, so keep the `Release`/`Acquire` atomics — they compile to `dmb`-fenced accesses that cost a few cycles at most here, and your code stays correct if it ever runs somewhere with real caches. Same story on Hazard3: RISC-V's weak model requires `fence` instructions architecturally even though this particular in-order implementation is docile. Rust's atomics do the right thing on both; don't hand-optimize them away.

**Atomicity is free where you need it.** Aligned 32-bit loads and stores are single-transaction on the fabric, so your `offset | 1` slot word is naturally atomic. And unlike the RP2040 (which famously had *no* exclusives, forcing the SIO hardware spinlocks for everything), the RP2350's M33s implement real ARMv8-M exclusives (`ldrex`/`strex`) with a global monitor, and Hazard3 implements the RISC-V A extension — so `AtomicU32` works natively. Your design needs none of that (no RMW, by construction), but it means the fallback paths exist.

**Placement knobs for your queue.** Two useful layouts: put the SPSC ring in striped SRAM so producer and consumer accesses statistically spread across banks, or deliberately place each core's stack/hot data in the dedicated 4 KB banks (SRAM8/SRAM9-equivalent) so the cores' background traffic never arbitrates against the shared ring at all. The latter is the embedded analogue of your isolcpus setup: partition by construction. Cache-line alignment padding is meaningless here (no lines, no false sharing), so you can drop the 64-byte alignment on this target — though keeping it costs only memory and keeps one codebase for the Zen 2 and RP2350 builds. The low-bits-free invariant for your tag bit survives either way since your pool slots will be at least 4-byte aligned.

**Also in the toolbox:** the SIO inter-core FIFOs — two hardware 32-bit×8-deep mailbox FIFOs, one per direction, with interrupt-on-nonempty. That's effectively a hardware SPSC of depth 8, and it's the natural "doorbell" if your consumer core sleeps (WFE/WFI) rather than spins: push the offset through your SRAM ring, tap the FIFO or use SEV to wake. For a spinning consumer, your tag-bit ring in SRAM is strictly more flexible (depth, payload discipline) and just as fast.

So the cross-platform picture for iiac-perf: Zen 2 same-CCX measures coherence-dominated handoff, Zen 2 same-core measures interrupt-path-dominated handoff, and RP2350 measures the floor where both terms vanish and you're left with raw instruction count plus a cycle of arbitration. Same Rust source, three very different histograms — which is exactly the portability story the acquire/release discipline buys you.

1	//! Shared setup for the `zcr-*` benches: leaked ring regions
2	//! and `'static` endpoint construction over the sibling
3	//! `zc-ring-x1` crate — the SPSC ring and its MPSC sibling.
4	
5	use zc_ring_x1::{
6	    CACHE_LINE_SIZE, Consumer, Header, MpscConsumer, MpscHeader, MpscProducer, MpscRing, Producer,
7	    Ring,
8	};
9	
10	/// Slot payload for every zcr bench: the round-trip counter.
11	/// `u64` satisfies the zerocopy bounds and matches the message
12	/// shape of the mpsc/ice benches.
13	pub type Msg = u64;
14	
15	/// Shutdown sentinel the 2t benches send instead of a counter
16	/// value; the echo worker exits on receipt without replying.
17	/// The counter increments skip it (see each bench's `step`).
18	pub const STOP: Msg = u64::MAX;
19	
20	/// Slots per ring — a power of two, comfortably above the one
21	/// message ever in flight in the round-trip benches.
22	pub const CAPACITY: u32 = 8;
23	
24	/// Region bytes: the four-cache-line [`Header`] plus
25	/// [`CAPACITY`] slots of one cache line each.
26	const REGION_BYTES: usize = size_of::<Header>() + CACHE_LINE_SIZE * CAPACITY as usize;
27	
28	/// Cache-line-aligned backing region for one ring, matching
29	/// `Ring::init`'s alignment requirement.
30	#[repr(C, align(64))]
31	struct Region([u8; REGION_BYTES]);
32	
33	/// Build a ring over a leaked region and split it into
34	/// `'static` endpoint handles.
35	///
36	/// - Leaked on purpose: the 2t benches move one endpoint into a
37	///   spawned worker thread, so the region must outlive the
38	///   bench struct. ~768 B per ring for the process lifetime is
39	///   fine in a bench binary.
40	pub fn leak_ring() -> (Producer<'static>, Consumer<'static>) {
41	    let region: &'static mut Region = Box::leak(Box::new(Region([0; REGION_BYTES])));
42	    Ring::init(&mut region.0, CACHE_LINE_SIZE as u32, CAPACITY)
43	        .expect("geometry is valid by construction")
44	        .split()
45	}
46	
47	/// MPSC region bytes: the [`MpscHeader`] plus the per-slot seq
48	/// array ([`CAPACITY`] × 4 B padded to a cache line) plus
49	/// [`CAPACITY`] slots of one cache line each.
50	const MPSC_REGION_BYTES: usize = size_of::<MpscHeader>()
51	    + (CAPACITY as usize * 4).next_multiple_of(CACHE_LINE_SIZE)
52	    + CACHE_LINE_SIZE * CAPACITY as usize;
53	
54	/// Cache-line-aligned backing region for one MPSC ring.
55	#[repr(C, align(64))]
56	struct MpscRegion([u8; MPSC_REGION_BYTES]);
57	
58	/// Build an MPSC ring over a leaked region and split it into
59	/// `'static` endpoint handles — the MPSC sibling of
60	/// [`leak_ring`], same leak rationale.
61	pub fn leak_mpsc_ring() -> (MpscProducer<'static>, MpscConsumer<'static>) {
62	    let region: &'static mut MpscRegion = Box::leak(Box::new(MpscRegion([0; MPSC_REGION_BYTES])));
63	    MpscRing::init(&mut region.0, CACHE_LINE_SIZE as u32, CAPACITY)
64	        .expect("geometry is valid by construction")
65	        .split()
66	}

# Versioning

How this project versions its commits and the running
artifact. The scheme — the cycle step-numbering and the
unique-per-commit aim — is generic and shared across projects:
this file is copied **verbatim**, with
[Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record)
covering each medium by conditional rather than per-project
edits.

## Terms

Three names, used as defined here across
[AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md),
[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md), and the notes files:

- **version** — the per-commit version (e.g. `0.3.0-5.3.0`),
  written with `-` in prose, ladders, chores, todo, and commit
  talk; its suffix encodes the cycle phase (see
  [Step numbering](#step-numbering)).
- **version-of-record** — the authoritative stored copy of the
  version, in the project's manifest (see
  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record));

- `X.Y.Z-3` — its Close-out

Design is clear and maps cleanly onto what's already here. Before I start, two forks that change the shape of the work.

**What I'd build** — a FastForward-style ring, in-repo as `src/ffq.rs`:

- Slot word = `AtomicUsize`; `0` = empty, `payload | 1` = full. No shared head/tail — producer and consumer each hold a private index. No RMW anywhere; on x86 both paths are plain `mov`.
- Payload is the existing `Msg = u64` counter stored as `msg << 1 | 1` (one shift per side) so the comparison against `zcr-*` is like-for-like, with a doc note that in the shm case the payload is a 64-B-aligned offset and the shift disappears.
- Benches `ffq-1t` and `ffq-2t` mirroring `zcr-with-1t` / `zcr-with-2t` exactly — same spin wait, same two-ring round trip, same `Drop`-sends-`STOP` shutdown — so it's a same-harness A/B against `zcr-with-2t` (137 ns) and `zcr-mpsc-2t`.
- Variants to measure: packed word slots vs 64-B-padded slots (your Q1 caveat about producer and consumer sharing one line near-empty), and the `--pin` sweep for free — `--pin 0,1` same-CCX vs `--pin 0,8` cross-CCX on the 3900X.

Two things from the conversation I'd deliberately **not** do now: same-core two-threads (both sides spin, so it livelocks — the interrupt-preempt handoff needs an actual ISR; `ffq-1t` is the no-coherence data point instead), and the RP2350 port. Also worth noting: the "silence histogram" diagnostic in A3 is essentially what rung 0.23.0-4 (environment grade from warmup) is building, so the isolation work has a home already.

Your 3 Pico Plus 2s: the RP2350 story in A5 is real and this design ports as-is, but that's a separate cycle — cross-compile target, no harness there yet.

1	Here is the convo, arduously copy/pasted, link to an extension I can use in the future. Also note, I have 3 Pimoroni Pico Plus 2 right in front of me:
2	
3	Q1:
4	I'm thinking of a high performance SPSC where the buffer is cache aligned thus there are always unused lower bits in the "address" (either direct address or a byte offset). Can we use bit 0 as a full empty flag so there is no need a separate shared counter/index to the next free/last filled?
5	
6	A1:
7	Yes — and you've essentially re-derived the FastForward queue design (Giacomoni et al., PPoPP '08), which is a good sign because it's one of the fastest known SPSC structures. The key move is exactly what you're describing: put the full/empty state *in the slot itself*, and then you need no shared head/tail at all. Producer and consumer each keep a purely private local index that they increment modulo N. Producer: load slot with acquire, if "empty" then store `payload | 1` with release. Consumer: load with acquire, if bit 0 set, take payload, store "empty" (0) with release. No shared counters, no RMW instructions anywhere, no wasted slot to disambiguate full-vs-empty at wraparound, and full N capacity usable.
8	
9	The tag bit specifically earns its keep in your shared-memory case. With process-local pointers you can just use NULL as the empty sentinel and skip the bit. But for shm you'll be storing byte offsets into the segment, and offset 0 can be a valid location — so `offset | 1` = full, `0` = empty is clean, and your cache-aligned message pool guarantees the low 6 bits are free. It also composes nicely with your pre-allocated pool model: the slot word is the entire message handoff (zero-copy, pointer/offset is the payload), and a single 8-byte release store publishes both the data and the flag atomically, so there's no separate "write payload then write flag" ordering to manage. On x86 that's just a plain `mov` each way.
10	
11	Two caveats worth knowing before you benchmark it against zcr-mpsc in iiac-perf:
12	
13	The first is the failure mode if you were instead thinking of tagging a *shared* index word (one word holding "next free/last filled" plus a flag). Don't — that makes both threads write the same cache line and forces CAS/exchange, which throws away the whole single-writer-per-line advantage of SPSC. The per-slot-flag version is the right reading of your idea.
14	
15	The second is real, though: in the latency-critical near-empty regime (which is your steady state for an actor runtime), producer and consumer are always operating on the *same slot's* cache line, so every message costs a full coherence round trip — producer's store invalidates consumer's copy, consumer's read pulls it Shared, consumer's writeback invalidates producer's copy again. That's two-ish line transfers per message. The index-based design with cached indices (Rigtorp-style, where each side caches the other's index and only re-reads on apparent full/empty) has the same problem near-empty but amortizes beautifully under throughput load. FastForward's answer was "temporal slipping" — deliberately keeping the consumer a few slots behind — which buys throughput at the cost of latency, probably the wrong trade for you. In practice on a single Zen 2 CCX the ping-pong is ~40ish ns through L3, and the flag design still tends to win or tie at low occupancy because it touches exactly one line per message versus three (slot + two index lines) for the naive two-index version.
16	
17	One micro-refinement to consider measuring: since the consumer's writeback of `0` is one of the two coherence transfers, there's a variant where the consumer doesn't clear the slot and instead a per-lap parity bit distinguishes stale from fresh (`offset | lap_bit`), making slots producer-write-only. The catch is the producer then can't tell from the slot whether it's been consumed, so the consumer has to publish its index occasionally anyway — you end up hybrid. Worth an HDR histogram side-by-side, but I'd expect the plain FastForward-with-tag-bit version to be the sweet spot for your round-trip benchmark.
18	
19	Q2:
20	So on an X86-64 Intel or AMD can I assign the ISR to always run on a particular core and then assign the other end of the SPSC to be on that same core? If so there should be a decent chance that both sides will have a cache hit?
21	
22	A2:
23	Yes, both halves are pinnable, and the payoff is better than "decent chance" — it changes the cache story qualitatively.
24	
25	**Mechanics.** Thread side: `sched_setaffinity`/`pthread_setaffinity_np` to core X. IRQ side: write a mask to `/proc/irq/N/smp_affinity` (or `smp_affinity_list`) for that vector — MSI/MSI-X vectors are individually steerable, so a specific device interrupt can be nailed to core X. Two gotchas: kill or configure `irqbalance`, or it'll migrate the vector out from under you; and on modern kernels many drivers use threaded IRQs (or `force_irqthreads`), which splits the ISR into a tiny hard-irq top half plus a kernel thread (`irq/N-name`) — that thread has its own affinity you need to pin too, and it follows the hard-irq affinity by default but verify. If your "ISR" is actually user-space (UIO/VFIO with the eventfd reader, or your simulated one), it's just another thread pin.
26	
27	**The cache consequence.** Same core means the slot's cache line never migrates. Producer store leaves it Modified in the local L1; consumer load hits it there; consumer's clear keeps it Modified in place. Zero coherence transactions, zero invalidations — the ~40 ns Zen 2 ping-pong we discussed simply doesn't exist. Both sides hit L1 essentially always, modulo the ISR handler's own code and data evicting some of the consumer's working set (L1 is 32 KB; a lean handler barely dents it, a fat driver path can).
28	
29	**The memory model consequence, which is the fun part.** A single core observes its own stores in program order, and interrupts are precise — the ISR sees everything the interrupted thread did, and vice versa on return. So producer/consumer on one core is signal-handler semantics, not concurrency: you don't need *hardware* ordering at all, only compiler ordering. In Rust terms, keep the `Atomic*` types but every acquire/release could legally be `Relaxed`-plus-`compiler_fence` — and since x86 acquire/release loads/stores compile to plain `mov` anyway, just leave them as acquire/release and pay nothing. A1:

The key move is exactly what you're describing: put the full/empty state *in the slot itself*, and then you need no shared head/tail at all. Producer and consumer each keep a purely private local index that they increment modulo N. Producer: load slot with acquire, if "empty" then store `payload | 1` with release. Consumer: load with acquire, if bit 0 set, take payload, store "empty" (0) with release. No shared counters, no RMW instructions anywhere, no wasted slot to disambiguate full-vs-empty at wraparound, and full N capacity usable.

The tag bit specifically earns its keep in your shared-memory case. With process-local pointers you can just use NULL as the empty sentinel and skip the bit. But for shm you'll be storing byte offsets into the segment, and offset 0 can be a valid location — so `offset | 1` = full, `0` = empty is clean, and your cache-aligned message pool guarantees the low 6 bits are free. It also composes nicely with your pre-allocated pool model: the slot word is the entire message handoff (zero-copy, pointer/offset is the payload), and a single 8-byte release store publishes both the data and the flag atomically, so there's no separate "write payload then write flag" ordering to manage. Two caveats worth knowing before you benchmark it against zcr-mpsc in iiac-perf:

The first is the failure mode if you were instead thinking of tagging a *shared* index word (one word holding "next free/last filled" plus a flag). Don't — that makes both threads write the same cache line and forces CAS/exchange, which throws away the whole single-writer-per-line advantage of SPSC. The per-slot-flag version is the right reading of your idea.

The second is real, though: in the latency-critical near-empty regime (which is your steady state for an actor runtime), producer and consumer are always operating on the *same slot's* cache line, so every message costs a full coherence round trip — producer's store invalidates consumer's copy, consumer's read pulls it Shared, consumer's writeback invalidates producer's copy again. ## Q1: tag bit in the slot word instead of shared indices

I'm thinking of a high performance SPSC where the buffer is cache aligned thus there are always unused lower bits in the "address" (either direct address or a byte offset). Can we use bit 0 as a full empty flag so there is no need a separate shared counter/index to the next free/last filled?

### A1

Yes — and you've essentially re-derived the FastForward queue design (Giacomoni et al., PPoPP '08), which is a good sign because it's one of the fastest known SPSC structures. The key move is exactly what you're describing: put the full/empty state *in the slot itself*, and then you need no shared head/tail at all. Producer and consumer each keep a purely private local index that they increment modulo N. Producer: load slot with acquire, if "empty" then store `payload | 1` with release. Consumer: load with acquire, if bit 0 set, take payload, store "empty" (0) with release. No shared counters, no RMW instructions anywhere, no wasted slot to disambiguate full-vs-empty at wraparound, and full N capacity usable.

The tag bit specifically earns its keep in your shared-memory case. With process-local pointers you can just use NULL as the empty sentinel and skip the bit. But for shm you'll be storing byte offsets into the segment, and offset 0 can be a valid location — so `offset | 1` = full, `0` = empty is clean, and your cache-aligned message pool guarantees the low 6 bits are free. It also composes nicely with your pre-allocated pool model: the slot word is the entire message handoff (zero-copy, pointer/offset is the payload), and a single 8-byte release store publishes both the data and the flag atomically, so there's no separate "write payload then write flag" ordering to manage. Two caveats worth knowing before you benchmark it against zcr-mpsc in iiac-perf:

The first is the failure mode if you were instead thinking of tagging a *shared* index word (one word holding "next free/last filled" plus a flag). Don't — that makes both threads write the same cache line and forces CAS/exchange, which throws away the whole single-writer-per-line advantage of SPSC. The per-slot-flag version is the right reading of your idea.

The second is real, though: in the latency-critical near-empty regime (which is your steady state for an actor runtime), producer and consumer are always operating on the *same slot's* cache line, so every message costs a full coherence round trip — producer's store invalidates consumer's copy, consumer's read pulls it Shared, consumer's writeback invalidates producer's copy again. That's two-ish line transfers per message. The index-based design with cached indices (Rigtorp-style, where each side caches the other's index and only re-reads on apparent full/empty) has the same problem near-empty but amortizes beautifully under throughput load. FastForward's answer was "temporal slipping" — deliberately keeping the consumer a few slots behind — which buys throughput at the cost of latency, probably the wrong trade for you. In practice on a single Zen 2 CCX the ping-pong is ~40ish ns through L3, and the flag design still tends to win or tie at low occupancy because it touches exactly one line per message versus three (slot + two index lines) for the naive two-index version.

One micro-refinement to consider measuring: since the consumer's writeback of `0` is one of the two coherence transfers, there's a variant where the consumer doesn't clear the slot and instead a per-lap parity bit distinguishes stale from fresh (`offset | lap_bit`), making slots producer-write-only. The catch is the producer then can't tell from the slot whether it's been consumed, so the consumer has to publish its index occasionally anyway — you end up hybrid. Worth an HDR histogram side-by-side, but I'd expect the plain FastForward-with-tag-bit version to be the sweet spot for your round-trip benchmark.

## Q2: pinning an ISR and the consumer to the same core

So on an X86-64 Intel or AMD can I assign the ISR to always run on a particular core and then assign the other end of the SPSC to be on that same core? If so there should be a decent chance that both sides will have a cache hit?

### A2

Yes, both halves are pinnable, and the payoff is better than "decent chance" — it changes the cache story qualitatively.

**Mechanics.** Thread side: `sched_setaffinity`/`pthread_setaffinity_np` to core X. IRQ side: write a mask to `/proc/irq/N/smp_affinity` (or `smp_affinity_list`) for that vector — MSI/MSI-X vectors are individually steerable, so a specific device interrupt can be nailed to core X. If your "ISR" is actually user-space (UIO/VFIO with the eventfd reader, or your simulated one), it's just another thread pin.

**The cache consequence.** Same core means the slot's cache line never migrates. Producer store leaves it Modified in the local L1; consumer load hits it there; consumer's clear keeps it Modified in place. Zero coherence transactions, zero invalidations — the ~40 ns Zen 2 ping-pong we discussed simply doesn't exist. Both sides hit L1 essentially always, modulo the ISR handler's own code and data evicting some of the consumer's working set (L1 is 32 KB; a lean handler barely dents it, a fat driver path can).

**The memory model consequence, which is the fun part.** A single core observes its own stores in program order, and interrupts are precise — the ISR sees everything the interrupted thread did, and vice versa on return. So producer/consumer on one core is signal-handler semantics, not concurrency: you don't need *hardware* ordering at all, only compiler ordering. In Rust terms, keep the `Atomic*` types but every acquire/release could legally be `Relaxed`-plus-`compiler_fence` — and since x86 acquire/release loads/stores compile to plain `mov` anyway, just leave them as acquire/release and pay nothing. What you must never do on this layout is spin *inside the ISR* waiting on the consumer (drop-on-full only — the consumer cannot run while you're in the handler; you'd deadlock the core), but that was already your ISR constraint.

**The trade you're making.** You've eliminated coherence latency but serialized execution: the ISR now steals cycles from the consumer instead of running in parallel on another core, and the handoff latency becomes interrupt entry/exit plus scheduler-free resume — the consumer literally cannot observe the message until the ISR returns. For a spinning consumer that's excellent and very deterministic: interrupt fires, preempts the spin loop mid-`pause`, handler does one L1 store, `iret`, the very next slot load hits. Total added latency is the hardware interrupt path (~1–2 µs through the Linux hard-irq machinery, much less on bare metal/RTOS — this dwarfs any cache effect either way, which is worth internalizing: on Linux the interrupt path cost makes the same-core vs cross-core cache question mostly academic for real ISRs). Cross-core, by contrast, lets the handler and consumer overlap, which wins when the consumer does nontrivial per-message work at high rates.

**One config detail that matters more than the pinning:** keep that core in C0. If the consumer spins, fine. If it ever sleeps, an idle core in C6 adds tens of microseconds of wake latency to the interrupt — `cpuidle` limits (`cpu_dma_latency` / `idle=poll` on the isolated core) or the spinning consumer itself solves it. Combine with `isolcpus`/`nohz_full` on that core and you also stop the scheduler tick and other vectors from landing there, which is what actually cleans up the tail in your histograms.

So for the benchmark matrix this gives you a fifth configuration worth measuring: same-core (interrupt-preempt handoff, no coherence) vs same-CCX cross-core vs cross-CCX. My prediction: same-core wins on median and determinism for your steady-state timer case, cross-core same-CCX wins whenever consumer work per message exceeds roughly the coherence round trip, and the RP2350 version of this story (where "same core" means the M33 servicing the IRQ) will look like the bare-metal ideal of it.

That's exactly the stuff that shows up as the fat tail in a latency histogram — a `kworker` deciding to flush something on your core is a multi-microsecond hole.

The modern non-boot-param route is cgroup v2 `cpuset.cpus.partition=isolated`.
- **`nohz_full=X`**: stops the periodic scheduler tick on that core while it runs a single thread — removes the 100–1000 Hz timer interrupt that otherwise perforates your spin loop.
- **`rcu_nocbs=X`**: offloads RCU callbacks to threads you can pin elsewhere.
- **`irqaffinity=`** boot param plus per-vector `smp_affinity`: steer *default* IRQ placement away from the core, then pin only your device's vector to it.
- Residual `kworker`s: some per-CPU work can't be moved (writeback mostly can, via `/sys/bus/workqueue/devices/writeback/cpumask`), and `migration/X` and `ksoftirqd/X` will always exist but should be near-silent on an isolated tickless core.

What you can never exclude from userspace: SMIs (firmware-level, invisible to the kernel except via `turbostat`'s SMI counter — worth checking your board, some BIOSes fire them periodically for fan/EC polling) and, on the same-core-ISR layout from before, your own device's interrupt, which is of course the point.

Practical note for the benchmark: `isolcpus` + `nohz_full` + `rcu_nocbs` on two cores of one CCX gets you 99.99th percentiles that actually reflect the queue rather than the OS. And there's a diagnostic worth running once before trusting any numbers: pin a pure TSC-sampling spin loop on the isolated core and histogram the gaps between successive reads — any gap over ~a few hundred ns is an intrusion (tick, IRQ, SMI), and that "silence histogram" is your noise floor. If the noise floor isn't clean, no queue comparison on top of it is.

The RTOS/bare-metal contrast is basically why this matters for your flight-controller thinking: on the RP2350 you get core exclusivity by construction, and the Linux tuning above is an attempt to approximate that on a general-purpose kernel. `PREEMPT_RT` helps a different problem (bounded kernel preemption when you *do* take interrupts) but doesn't remove the intrusions — isolation does.

### A4

Yes, that's the right summary — with one attribution worth keeping straight: the two properties come from different sources.

The **queue design** (slot flag, private indices, one cache line per message) is what buys the better median and the *narrowness* of the main lobe. A two-index design has more moving parts whose costs depend on occupancy history, which smears the distribution even when nothing external intrudes.

The **tail density vs. tail length** distinction is exactly right, and it's governed by the environment, not the queue. The worst-case reading is set by the worst intrusion — an SMI, a stray IPI, a thermal event — and no queue structure shortens that; if a 50 µs SMI lands between produce and consume, that sample is 50 µs regardless of how elegant the handoff is. What isolation (isolcpus/nohz_full/rcu_nocbs/IRQ steering) does is reduce the *rate* of intrusions, thinning the tail's population without necessarily lowering its maximum. And the queue design contributes a little here too, indirectly: fewer instructions and fewer cache lines per message means a smaller time window per handoff during which an intrusion can land *inside* the measurement, so marginally fewer samples get contaminated at all.

So the histogram you should expect: tall narrow mode at the L1-or-one-coherence-hop latency, a small deterministic shoulder (the "consumer just missed it and looped once" case), then a sparse scatter of environment-caused outliers whose *positions* are about the same as any other design's but whose *count* is low. The honest way to report it — and the useful iiac-perf output — is percentiles plus max as separate claims: p50/p99/p99.9 reflect your design, max reflects your platform. If someone (including future-you) compares queues by max alone on a non-isolated box, they're measuring the kernel, not the queue.

One falsifiable check to close the loop: run the same queue on isolated vs. non-isolated cores. Design effects should leave p50 nearly identical and mostly reshape p99.9+; if p50 moves a lot between those runs, something else is wrong (frequency scaling, C-states, wrong core pairing).

**The memory system.** Each core (whether you've booted the Cortex-M33s or the Hazard3 RISC-V cores — the selection is per-socket at boot, two running at once in any mix) talks straight to SRAM through a crossbar bus fabric. The 520 KB of SRAM is split into 10 banks: 8 large banks that are word-striped by default (consecutive words rotate across banks, spreading load), plus 2 small 4 KB direct-mapped banks intended as core-local scratch. Every access is uncached and single-cycle *when unarbitrated*. The only cache in the system is the XIP cache in front of QSPI flash — and since it sits in the fabric, both cores go *through the same cache*, so it's coherent by unification rather than by protocol. (The one sharp edge: if you write flash or use the XIP window in exotic ways, there are cache maintenance ops, but that's code, not your data path.)

**What replaces coherence traffic: arbitration.** Two masters (cores, plus DMA) hitting the *same bank* in the same cycle stall one of them for a cycle. That's the entire contention story — no MESI states, no invalidations, no line migration, no ping-pong. Your SPSC slot word being hammered by both cores costs at most occasional single-cycle arbitration stalls, deterministic and tiny. **Ordering still matters architecturally, though.** No caches doesn't mean no memory model. The M33 is in-order and in practice doesn't reorder your stores, but ARMv8-M *permits* reordering to Normal memory, so keep the `Release`/`Acquire` atomics — they compile to `dmb`-fenced accesses that cost a few cycles at most here, and your code stays correct if it ever runs somewhere with real caches. Same story on Hazard3: RISC-V's weak model requires `fence` instructions architecturally even though this particular in-order implementation is docile. Rust's atomics do the right thing on both; don't hand-optimize them away.

**Atomicity is free where you need it.** Aligned 32-bit loads and stores are single-transaction on the fabric, so your `offset | 1` slot word is naturally atomic. And unlike the RP2040 (which famously had *no* exclusives, forcing the SIO hardware spinlocks for everything), the RP2350's M33s implement real ARMv8-M exclusives (`ldrex`/`strex`) with a global monitor, and Hazard3 implements the RISC-V A extension — so `AtomicU32` works natively. Your design needs none of that (no RMW, by construction), but it means the fallback paths exist.

**Placement knobs for your queue.** Two useful layouts: put the SPSC ring in striped SRAM so producer and consumer accesses statistically spread across banks, or deliberately place each core's stack/hot data in the dedicated 4 KB banks (SRAM8/SRAM9-equivalent) so the cores' background traffic never arbitrates against the shared ring at all. The latter is the embedded analogue of your isolcpus setup: partition by construction. Cache-line alignment padding is meaningless here (no lines, no false sharing), so you can drop the 64-byte alignment on this target — though keeping it costs only memory and keeps one codebase for the Zen 2 and RP2350 builds. The low-bits-free invariant for your tag bit survives either way since your pool slots will be at least 4-byte aligned.

Right — you've got the direction of the guarantee correct. Affinity constrains where *that thread* may run; it says nothing about what else runs on that core. By default core X still gets: other runnable user threads (the scheduler happily load-balances onto it), per-CPU kernel threads (`ksoftirqd/X`, `kworker/X:*`, `migration/X`, `rcu` machinery), the scheduler tick, timer callbacks, other IRQ vectors, and TLB-shootdown/function-call IPIs from the rest of the system. That's exactly the stuff that shows up as the fat tail in a latency histogram — a `kworker` deciding to flush something on your core is a multi-microsecond hole.

Making the core effectively exclusive is a stack of opt-outs, roughly in order of impact:

- **`isolcpus=X`** (or cpusets / `cset shield`, or systemd `CPUAffinity=` for everything else): removes the core from the general scheduler domain, so only explicitly-pinned threads land there. This is the "possibility" you're gesturing at — it exists but is opt-in at boot or via cgroup partitioning, not implied by affinity. The modern non-boot-param route is cgroup v2 `cpuset.cpus.partition=isolated`.
- **`nohz_full=X`**: stops the periodic scheduler tick on that core while it runs a single thread — removes the 100–1000 Hz timer interrupt that otherwise perforates your spin loop.
- **`rcu_nocbs=X`**: offloads RCU callbacks to threads you can pin elsewhere.
- **`irqaffinity=`** boot param plus per-vector `smp_affinity`: steer *default* IRQ placement away from the core, then pin only your device's vector to it.
- Residual `kworker`s: some per-CPU work can't be moved (writeback mostly can, via `/sys/bus/workqueue/devices/writeback/cpumask`), and `migration/X` and `ksoftirqd/X` will always exist but should be near-silent on an isolated tickless core.

What you can never exclude from userspace: SMIs (firmware-level, invisible to the kernel except via `turbostat`'s SMI counter — worth checking your board, some BIOSes fire them periodically for fan/EC polling) and, on the same-core-ISR layout from before, your own device's interrupt, which is of course the point.

Practical note for the benchmark: `isolcpus` + `nohz_full` + `rcu_nocbs` on two cores of one CCX gets you 99.99th percentiles that actually reflect the queue rather than the OS. And there's a diagnostic worth running once before trusting any numbers: pin a pure TSC-sampling spin loop on the isolated core and histogram the gaps between successive reads — any gap over ~a few hundred ns is an intrusion (tick, IRQ, SMI), and that "silence histogram" is your noise floor. If the noise floor isn't clean, no queue comparison on top of it is.

The RTOS/bare-metal contrast is basically why this matters for your flight-controller thinking: on the RP2350 you get core exclusivity by construction, and the Linux tuning above is an attempt to approximate that on a general-purpose kernel. `PREEMPT_RT` helps a different problem (bounded kernel preemption when you *do* take interrupts) but doesn't remove the intrusions — isolation does.

## Q4: expected histogram shape — tail density vs tail length

Sooo I can construct an SPSC that uses bit 0 for used/available and even in the "poll" case it will have much better performance and narrower histogram and the long tail will be less dense. It may not be shorter, in the worse case, but fewer readings in the long tail?

### A4

Yes, that's the right summary — with one attribution worth keeping straight: the two properties come from different sources.

The **queue design** (slot flag, private indices, one cache line per message) is what buys the better median and the *narrowness* of the main lobe. The polling fast path is a single acquire load that either hits L1 (same-core or quiet slot) or costs one deterministic coherence transfer (cross-core). There's no shared-index line to contend on, no RMW whose latency varies with contention, no "re-read the other side's index" slow path that fires data-dependently. Fewer variable-latency operations per message = tighter distribution, almost by construction. A two-index design has more moving parts whose costs depend on occupancy history, which smears the distribution even when nothing external intrudes.

The **tail density vs. tail length** distinction is exactly right, and it's governed by the environment, not the queue. The worst-case reading is set by the worst intrusion — an SMI, a stray IPI, a thermal event — and no queue structure shortens that; if a 50 µs SMI lands between produce and consume, that sample is 50 µs regardless of how elegant the handoff is. What isolation (isolcpus/nohz_full/rcu_nocbs/IRQ steering) does is reduce the *rate* of intrusions, thinning the tail's population without necessarily lowering its maximum. And the queue design contributes a little here too, indirectly: fewer instructions and fewer cache lines per message means a smaller time window per handoff during which an intrusion can land *inside* the measurement, so marginally fewer samples get contaminated at all.

So the histogram you should expect: tall narrow mode at the L1-or-one-coherence-hop latency, a small deterministic shoulder (the "consumer just missed it and looped once" case), then a sparse scatter of environment-caused outliers whose *positions* are about the same as any other design's but whose *count* is low. The honest way to report it — and the useful iiac-perf output — is percentiles plus max as separate claims: p50/p99/p99.9 reflect your design, max reflects your platform. If someone (including future-you) compares queues by max alone on a non-isolated box, they're measuring the kernel, not the queue.

One falsifiable check to close the loop: run the same queue on isolated vs. non-isolated cores. Design effects should leave p50 nearly identical and mostly reshape p99.9+; if p50 moves a lot between those runs, something else is wrong (frequency scaling, C-states, wrong core pairing).

## Q5: RP2350 cache coherence architecture

On an RP2350 there are 4 cores 2 ARM, 2 RISC-V of which only 2 run at once, what are its cache coherence architecture?

### A5

Short answer: it doesn't have one, because it doesn't need one — there are no per-core data caches to keep coherent. This makes the RP2350 the degenerate (and pleasant) case of everything we've been discussing.

**The memory system.** Each core (whether you've booted the Cortex-M33s or the Hazard3 RISC-V cores — the selection is per-socket at boot, two running at once in any mix) talks straight to SRAM through a crossbar bus fabric. The 520 KB of SRAM is split into 10 banks: 8 large banks that are word-striped by default (consecutive words rotate across banks, spreading load), plus 2 small 4 KB direct-mapped banks intended as core-local scratch. Every access is uncached and single-cycle *when unarbitrated*. The only cache in the system is the XIP cache in front of QSPI flash — and since it sits in the fabric, both cores go *through the same cache*, so it's coherent by unification rather than by protocol. (The one sharp edge: if you write flash or use the XIP window in exotic ways, there are cache maintenance ops, but that's code, not your data path.)

**What replaces coherence traffic: arbitration.** Two masters (cores, plus DMA) hitting the *same bank* in the same cycle stall one of them for a cycle. That's the entire contention story — no MESI states, no invalidations, no line migration, no ping-pong. Your SPSC slot word being hammered by both cores costs at most occasional single-cycle arbitration stalls, deterministic and tiny. This is why the RP2350 histogram will look like the platonic ideal of your benchmark: the "coherence round trip" term is literally zero, and the tail intrusions are only interrupts you chose to enable.

**Ordering still matters architecturally, though.** No caches doesn't mean no memory model. The M33 is in-order and in practice doesn't reorder your stores, but ARMv8-M *permits* reordering to Normal memory, so keep the `Release`/`Acquire` atomics — they compile to `dmb`-fenced accesses that cost a few cycles at most here, and your code stays correct if it ever runs somewhere with real caches. Same story on Hazard3: RISC-V's weak model requires `fence` instructions architecturally even though this particular in-order implementation is docile. Rust's atomics do the right thing on both; don't hand-optimize them away.

**Atomicity is free where you need it.** Aligned 32-bit loads and stores are single-transaction on the fabric, so your `offset | 1` slot word is naturally atomic. And unlike the RP2040 (which famously had *no* exclusives, forcing the SIO hardware spinlocks for everything), the RP2350's M33s implement real ARMv8-M exclusives (`ldrex`/`strex`) with a global monitor, and Hazard3 implements the RISC-V A extension — so `AtomicU32` works natively. Your design needs none of that (no RMW, by construction), but it means the fallback paths exist.

**Placement knobs for your queue.** Two useful layouts: put the SPSC ring in striped SRAM so producer and consumer accesses statistically spread across banks, or deliberately place each core's stack/hot data in the dedicated 4 KB banks (SRAM8/SRAM9-equivalent) so the cores' background traffic never arbitrates against the shared ring at all. The latter is the embedded analogue of your isolcpus setup: partition by construction. Cache-line alignment padding is meaningless here (no lines, no false sharing), so you can drop the 64-byte alignment on this target — though keeping it costs only memory and keeps one codebase for the Zen 2 and RP2350 builds. The low-bits-free invariant for your tag bit survives either way since your pool slots will be at least 4-byte aligned.

**Also in the toolbox:** the SIO inter-core FIFOs — two hardware 32-bit×8-deep mailbox FIFOs, one per direction, with interrupt-on-nonempty. That's effectively a hardware SPSC of depth 8, and it's the natural "doorbell" if your consumer core sleeps (WFE/WFI) rather than spins: push the offset through your SRAM ring, tap the FIFO or use SEV to wake. For a spinning consumer, your tag-bit ring in SRAM is strictly more flexible (depth, payload discipline) and just as fast.

So the cross-platform picture for iiac-perf: Zen 2 same-CCX measures coherence-dominated handoff, Zen 2 same-core measures interrupt-path-dominated handoff, and RP2350 measures the floor where both terms vanish and you're left with raw instruction count plus a cycle of arbitration. Same Rust source, three very different histograms — which is exactly the portability story the acquire/release discipline buys you.

vc-x1 0.71.0

Commit both repos, push the work repo's BOOKMARK, and
squash-push the bot repo's `main` — one resumable command.

Collapses the manual commit-push-publish ceremony into a
single subcommand with two interactive approval gates and a
state machine with persistent progress so interruptions can
resume without re-doing completed stages.

Stages: preflight (tracking / bot-published / sync checks —
no build steps; run project checks yourself before pushing)
→ review (approve diff)
→ message ($EDITOR / --title+--body, approve text) →
commit-work → commit-bot (skipped if clean) → bookmark-set
(work repo → <bookmark>, bot repo → main) → push-work →
squash-push-bot. Failures in commit-work / commit-bot /
bookmark-set roll both repos back via
`jj op restore` to the snapshot recorded before commit-work.
After push-work succeeds the remote boundary is crossed and
recovery is forward-only.

Non-interactive use: pass both --title and --body plus --yes
to skip the review gate. Saved state carries title/body
across resumes so only the first invocation needs them.

Usage: vc-x1 push [OPTIONS] [BOOKMARK]

Arguments:
  [BOOKMARK]
          Bookmark to advance in the work repo (positional form of
          `--bookmark`). The bot repo always advances `main`.
          
          Accepting a positional lets the common case read as `vc-x1 push main`
          without the `--bookmark` ceremony; `--bookmark` is kept as an alias
          for scripts and for composition with other args. The two forms
          conflict if both supplied.

Thoughts only — nothing run beyond three read-only checks.

**Two mechanical corrections to the plan as written.**

`jj edit zymwpvmn` will be refused. `main` and `main@origin` are the same commit, so it's inside jj's default immutable set (`trunk()`), and `jj edit` on an immutable commit errors out. What you want is **`jj new main`** — a fresh empty working copy on main, which is exactly the "reposition @ back" you're describing.

`vc-x1 push <bookmark>` does take the positional, and it sets the bookmark itself (stage `bookmark-set`), so you don't need `jj bookmark create` first. The one unknown: preflight includes a tracking check, and a brand-new bookmark has no remote counterpart to track. `web-claude-tweaks` exists, so the path has probably been walked before — but if preflight complains, that's why.

**The versioning precedent you already set.** `web-claude-tweaks` carries `version = "0.21.0-b"` — a letter suffix, which is how you numbered an off-ladder commit last time. versioning.md doesn't document letters (only `-0`, `-N`, bare), so if this becomes a habit it should get written down. Either way `Cargo.toml` needs a bump before any commit here: it currently reads `0.23.0-3`, which is the already-pushed -3 commit's version, so committing as-is would duplicate it.

**The part I'd push back on: should this be a branch?**

The cost is concrete. TODO.md #2 is only useful when someone reads TODO.md, and on a topic branch nobody does — including future-you opening the file to pick the next item. Meanwhile the 0.23.0 ladder continues on main and every rung edits TODO.md, so the branch diverges immediately in the single most-edited file in the repo, and the merge conflicts there. `web-claude-tweaks` has been parked since 2026-07-24 and has earned its own Todo (now #6) to rebase it. A second stranded branch makes that a pattern.

Three ways to go, in the order I'd pick them:

- **Fold it into the 0.23.0-4 commit.** No branch, no version invention, no merge debt, and the Todo entry lands on main where it does its job. Cost is one commit body carrying two file bullets that aren't about the environment grade — mild, and the commit body is file-by-file anyway. Best if -4 is coming up soon.
- **Land on main now as `0.23.0-a`.** If you want it published *today* rather than whenever -4 is written. Inserts a non-rung commit between -3 and -4, so the version-of-record reads 0.23.0-3 → 0.23.0-a → 0.23.0-4, which is odd-looking but unambiguous — and it's what the letter suffix appears to be for. Bookmark stays `main`, then `jj new main` isn't even needed since push leaves you on a fresh working copy.
- **Topic branch as you proposed** — `ffq-spsc-notes` (or `spsc-qa-notes`), title something like `docs: archive SPSC Q&A, add ffq Todo`. Right answer only if you specifically want this *off* main — which for a pure notes addition with zero code coupling I can't see a reason for.

Two smaller notes if you do branch: the bot repo always squash-pushes to its own `main`, so the session record lands on main with an `ochid` pointing into the branch — that survives a later rebase, since the chid travels with the commit and only the SHA changes. And per AGENTS.md, don't backfill a `Commits:` ref for a branch commit until the branch lands; nothing to backfill here (both new refs are file paths, not commit URLs), but it bites the moment this grows a chores section.

1	//! Hardware tick counter abstraction: thin wrapper over the
2	//! target architecture's fixed-rate monotonic counter.
3	//!
4	//! Probes call three functions; the per-arch impl lives in a
5	//! child module gated by `#[cfg(target_arch = ...)]`:
6	//!
7	//! - [`read_ticks`] — current counter value.
8	//! - [`ticks_per_ns`] — calibrated conversion ratio.
9	//! - [`require_ok`] — exit the process if the counter isn't
10	//!   usable for probe measurements.
11	//!
12	//! `x86_64` (`rdtsc`) and `aarch64` (`CNTVCT_EL0`) are
13	//! implemented today. RISC-V (`time` CSR) has an architecturally
14	//! invariant counter by ISA spec, so its `require_ok` will be
15	//! (nearly) a no-op once that impl lands.
16	
17	#[cfg(target_arch = "x86_64")]
18	mod x86_64;
19	
20	#[cfg(target_arch = "x86_64")]
21	use x86_64 as imp;
22	
23	#[cfg(target_arch = "aarch64")]
24	mod aarch64;
25	
26	#[cfg(target_arch = "aarch64")]
27	use aarch64 as imp;

32	     and \"aarch64\". Add a per-arch impl module (RISC-V: time CSR) \
33	     and wire it into src/ticks.rs."
34	);

39	    imp::read_ticks()
40	}

43	/// (x86_64) or read from hardware (aarch64, `CNTFRQ_EL0`).
44	/// Cached — the first call does the work.
