# Chores 05

Continuation of [chores-04](chores-04.md). Records landed work;
conventions in [AGENTS.md](../../AGENTS.md#chores-conventions) and
[cycle-protocol.md](../cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections).

## feat: grade the run from raw batches

Commits: [[1]],[[2]],[[3]]

Decided in
[Replanning II](chores-04.md#replanning-ii-drop-the-adjustment-grade-the-run):
the overhead subtraction estimates an ill-defined quantity —
additivity is an approximation on a superscalar CPU, the
constants moved ~10% with frequency regimes, and the correction
cancels in same-harness A/B anyway — while the calibration-time
grade certified a ~1 s window *before* the run: the room, not
the exam. This cycle removes the adjustment machinery and moves
grading onto the run's own time-ordered batch data.

### As-built ladder

- [[1]] 0.23.0-0 `chore: open raw-batch grading cycle`
- [[2]] 0.23.0-1 `feat: micro-probe inner-loop sizing` —
  `pick_inner`'s frame input now comes from a ~1 ms
  micro-probe (low quantile over back-to-back timer pairs)
  instead of `cfg.overhead.frame_call_ns`; sizing no longer
  depends on startup calibration. Also lands
  `tests/settle_anomaly.rs`, the `#[ignore]`d settle-anomaly
  acceptance test for the dynamic-warmup Todo — captured
  while the failing baseline (calibrate letter) still exists
  — and per-signal letters on the environment line
  (`CalGrade::signal_letters`), a display shakedown for the
  -4 gauge: every composite letter now names its cause
- [[3]] 0.23.0-2 `feat: time-ordered batch pipeline` —
  samples flow through `BatchPipeline` (raw buffer, flush on
  65,536 samples or 50 ms, whichever first): per-batch
  summaries (floor, mean, max, census over-floor count,
  timestamps) for the -3 gauge, then bulk-record into the
  histogram, buffer reused; memory bounded. Block mode
  flushes at block boundaries so no batch spans a sleep gap.
  Run outputs folded into `RunOutput` (retiring
  print_report's too-many-arguments debt); header gains
  `batches=N`
- [[N]] 0.23.0-3 `feat: batch-based run gauge` — `gauge.rs`
  grades a run from its batch series and prints a `run` row
  with the letter and all four signals, each carrying its own
  letter, with the composite on its own `overall worst case:`
  line beneath them. Landed beside the calibration grade so the
  two can be read against each other; four signals to
  calibration's six, see
  [Six calibration signals, four run signals](#six-calibration-signals-four-run-signals).
  It reports and never warns — see
  [Grade the run, judge the box](#grade-the-run-judge-the-box).

- [[N]] 0.23.0-4 `feat: environment grade from warmup` —
  `EnvGrade` grades the **box** from a series of
  micro-probes taken during warmup, and prints as its own
  `env` row above the run row. The probes measure the
  apparatus alone, so the letter carries no workload
  character — the separation the run grade's "reports, never
  warns" stance asked for. The single sizing probe becomes a
  16-probe series interleaved with the warmup steps, with the
  last one feeding `pick_inner` as before; see
  [Grading the box without the bench](#grading-the-box-without-the-bench)
  and
  [Why the probe times groups](#why-the-probe-times-groups).
  `overall worst case:` is renamed `run worst case:` now that
  two grades print

### Grading the box without the bench

The run grade describes the run it printed, and a run's
steadiness is largely its workload's character. That is the
right answer for a histogram's caption and the wrong one for
the question "is this machine fit to measure on" — the
question the retired `calibrate` grade was really answering,
and the one -6 removes an answer to.

Warmup is the only window a run has where no workload has
entered the numbers yet, so that is where the environment
certificate is measured. The probe times timer pairs and
nothing else, which is what makes the resulting letter a
statement about the machine.

Signals against the run grade's four:

- `interference`, `drift`, `step` — the same questions with
  the same definitions, over a different population. `drift`
  is the one the cycle needs most: it is the frequency-ramp
  detector the 7600x F diagnosis and the 3900X bistability
  both call for.
- `spread` — new here: how wide a probe's bulk sits above its
  own floor. There is no run-side analog worth having,
  because a bench's spread is mostly its workload (park /
  unpark bimodality is a fact about `mpsc`, not the box)
  while a timer pair has no character of its own.
- `bursts` — dropped. At 16 probes the hot-fraction is
  granular to 1/16, and the contamination it would count is
  already counted by `interference` at group resolution.

Thresholds are separate from the run grade's even where the
numbers currently match, because the two grade different
populations and should be free to diverge as measurement
says they should.

### Why the probe times groups

The probe's unit of measurement changed from a single timer
pair to a *group* of 64 pairs, timed by one outer `Instant`
pair and divided down.

The reason is resolution. The timer reads integer
nanoseconds, so a single ~25 ns pair is quantized to ~4% —
coarser than the ~9% bistable shift the environment grade
exists to see, which would have left `spread` reporting
quantization and `drift` unable to resolve anything smaller
than a P-state jump. A 64-pair group totals ~1.6 µs, so the
same 1 ns quantum is ~0.06% of the value and the per-pair
figure lands on a ~15 ps lattice. Measured on the 3900X the
difference is visible directly: `spread` reads 0.37% on a
quiet box, well clear of a floor that single-pair timing
would have pinned near 4%.

Total work is unchanged (32,768 pairs, ~1 ms), and the
sizing input shifts only in spirit — from "the quietest
single pair" to "the mean pair of the quietest group". Both
are an uncontended frame cost, which is all `pick_inner`
documents itself as needing.

### The two grades against each other

First numbers on the 3900X, `min-now -d 3`, both grades
printing side by side:

- Quiet box: `env` A (spread 0.37%, interference 0.31%,
  drift 0.00%, step 0.00%) beside `run` A. The
  still-surviving `calibrate` grade read B on the same run,
  its `resid 1.38% B` — a fit-quality signal with no
  environment analog by construction, so the disagreement is
  the expected kind.
- Six background spinners: `env` D (drift 5.22%, step 5.19%
  @0.015s) beside `run` D (drift 5.45%, step 5.45% @0.9s).
  Both grades caught the same disturbance independently,
  each on its own population and its own clock — the
  environment one 0.9 s earlier, because warmup precedes the
  run.

We think that second row is the useful cross-check: an
environment D with a run D says the box moved under the
measurement, while an environment A with a run D would say
the workload is bursty on a quiet machine. Distinguishing
those two was the point of splitting the grades.

### Grading the box without the bench

The run grade describes the run it printed, and a run's
steadiness is largely its workload's character. That is the
right answer for a histogram's caption and the wrong one for
the question "is this machine fit to measure on" — the
question the retired `calibrate` grade was really answering,
and the one -6 removes an answer to.

Warmup is the only window a run has where no workload has
entered the numbers yet, so that is where the environment
certificate is measured. The probe times timer pairs and
nothing else, which is what makes the resulting letter a
statement about the machine.

Signals against the run grade's four:

- `interference`, `drift`, `step` — the same questions with
  the same definitions, over a different population. `drift`
  is the one the cycle needs most: it is the frequency-ramp
  detector the 7600x F diagnosis and the 3900X bistability
  both call for.
- `spread` — new here: how wide a probe's bulk sits above its
  own floor. There is no run-side analog worth having,
  because a bench's spread is mostly its workload (park /
  unpark bimodality is a fact about `mpsc`, not the box)
  while a timer pair has no character of its own.
- `bursts` — dropped. At 16 probes the hot-fraction is
  granular to 1/16, and the contamination it would count is
  already counted by `interference` at group resolution.

Thresholds are separate from the run grade's even where the
numbers currently match, because the two grade different
populations and should be free to diverge as measurement
says they should.

### Why the probe times groups

The probe's unit of measurement changed from a single timer
pair to a *group* of 64 pairs, timed by one outer `Instant`
pair and divided down.

The reason is resolution. The timer reads integer
nanoseconds, so a single ~25 ns pair is quantized to ~4% —
coarser than the ~9% bistable shift the environment grade
exists to see, which would have left `spread` reporting
quantization and `drift` unable to resolve anything smaller
than a P-state jump. A 64-pair group totals ~1.6 µs, so the
same 1 ns quantum is ~0.06% of the value and the per-pair
figure lands on a ~15 ps lattice. Measured on the 3900X the
difference is visible directly: `spread` reads 0.37% on a
quiet box, well clear of a floor that single-pair timing
would have pinned near 4%.

Total work is unchanged (32,768 pairs, ~1 ms), and the
sizing input shifts only in spirit — from "the quietest
single pair" to "the mean pair of the quietest group". Both
are an uncontended frame cost, which is all `pick_inner`
documents itself as needing.

### The two grades against each other

First numbers on the 3900X, `min-now -d 3`, both grades
printing side by side:

- Quiet box: `env` A (spread 0.37%, interference 0.31%,
  drift 0.00%, step 0.00%) beside `run` A. The
  still-surviving `calibrate` grade read B on the same run,
  its `resid 1.38% B` — a fit-quality signal with no
  environment analog by construction, so the disagreement is
  the expected kind.
- Six background spinners: `env` D (drift 5.22%, step 5.19%
  @0.015s) beside `run` D (drift 5.45%, step 5.45% @0.9s).
  Both grades caught the same disturbance independently,
  each on its own population and its own clock — the
  environment one 0.9 s earlier, because warmup precedes the
  run.

We think that second row is the useful cross-check: an
environment D with a run D says the box moved under the
measurement, while an environment A with a run D would say
the workload is bursty on a quiet machine. Distinguishing
those two was the point of splitting the grades.

content.text: Good instinct — that's worth chasing rather than accepting. Let me check the one structural thing that would explain it.

Your suspicion is well-founded. Three findings, one of which is structural.

**1. The env grade is measured on a box that calibration already warmed.** `main.rs:617` runs `overhead::calibrate()` — about a second of hard spinning — before the bench loop at line 744. Every bench's warmup, and therefore every env probe, runs after that. So the frequency governor is already at the top when the probes start. The grade can't see a cold-start ramp because there isn't one left to see. That resolves at -6 when `calibrate` is deleted, and the A's you're looking at are partly an artifact of the demolition not having happened yet.

**2. The window is ~17 ms.** Sixteen probes at ~1 ms, plus 10,000 min-now steps at 24 ns (~0.24 ms). Against governor ramps the notes put at tens-to-hundreds of ms, that's short — and `drift` over 17 ms is not the same quantity as the run grade's `drift` over 5 s, despite printing in the same units on the adjacent line. This cycle's own critique of the calibration grade was that it certified the room and not the exam; a 17 ms environment certificate is a smaller version of the same problem. I should have caught that before showing you two A's.

`drift 0.00%` is not a rounded-down small number, incidentally: the floor lattice is ~15.6 ps, so any movement at all would print as ≥0.06%. The floors across those 16 probes are bit-identical. On a fully-warmed box over 17 ms that's believable — it's just a much weaker claim than "the 3900X is steady".

**3. Grouping cost the census its sensitivity.** This one is my error in the tradeoff. The census cut is `max(1.5 × floor, floor + 5 ns)`, applied to a *group mean*. A group is 64 pairs totalling ~1.6 µs, so a group only counts as disturbed if it absorbs ~800 ns of extra time — an 8x-blunter instrument than the run grade's per-sample census, which is why `env interference` reads lower than `run interference` for the same box. Fixable cheaply and without giving up resolution: each pair's own `elapsed()` is already computed inside the group loop and currently discarded, so counting per-pair intrusions costs nothing. A census threshold sits far above the 1 ns quantization, so pair-level counting is unaffected by the problem that drove grouping in the first place. Floor/spread/drift/step keep using group means.

**What I'd do:** take the census fix regardless — it's strictly better. The window is the real fork:

- **Leave it and document the scope** — the letter means "the box was steady across warmup", full stop, and it grows teeth at -6 when calibration stops pre-warming, and again when the Dynamic startup warmup Todo lengthens the window to convergence. Least work, and the honest reading of what -4 is: the certificate that must exist before -6, not yet the final instrument.
- **Probe across the whole run** — interleave a micro-probe between batches so the env series spans the same seconds the run grade does, making the two directly comparable on one timeline. Strictly the better instrument, and it keeps the workload-independence property since probes still time only timer pairs. Costs a little bench time and perturbs the run slightly, and it's a bigger change than the rung called for.

The plain version: the grade says "this machine was quiet" — but it only watched for about a sixtieth of a second, right after a second of hard work had already woken the machine up. So the A is true and it isn't worth much yet. Two of the reasons are temporary and go away later in this cycle; one is a mistake in how I count interruptions, and I'd like to fix that one now either way.

aiTitle: Implement and measure high performance SPSC queue

content.text:
Your suggestion didn't get lost — it landed, but only on half the problem. The batch pipeline (-2) and run gauge (-3) are exactly that design: raw samples accumulate in a block, the block is summarized (floor, mean, census) *before* being bulk-recorded into the histogram, buffer reused, memory bounded. That's why `run:` already covers the whole `--duration` and the histogram still gets every sample. What I built at -4 failed to apply the same idea to the environment side — I put the probes only in warmup, which is why you're looking at a 17 ms certificate next to a 5 s one.

The fix is to give the env probe the batch cadence: one short micro-probe at each batch flush seam. The seam is already a natural stopping point — the pipeline pauses there to summarize, and it already knows how to move the batch clock past a gap (it does that for block sleeps, so no batch spans time the bench wasn't running). Sizing still reads the last warmup probe, so `pick_inner` is untouched.

**Cost and shape.** With ~120 batches in a 5 s run, each probe can be far shorter than the current one — 128 groups of 64 pairs is ~256 µs, about 0.5% of run time, and still enough population for a p10/p90. You'd get ~120 box floors on the same time axis as ~120 bench floors, instead of 16 floors on a separate 17 ms axis. Keep the warmup probes too: cold-start ramp only exists there, and that's the part that grows teeth at -6. Anchored to one origin the two stretches form a single continuous series, so `drift` becomes "did the box move between warmup and the end of the run" — the question worth asking.

**The payoff you may not have been aiming at.** Once every batch carries both a bench floor and a box floor *at the same instant*, the two series can be correlated, and the report can attribute movement instead of just reporting it. Bench floor moves and box floor moves with it: the machine did that. Bench floor moves and the box floor doesn't: the workload did that. Neither grade alone can distinguish those — it needs the shared time axis, which this gets for free. That's a stronger result than either letter, and I think it's the real reason to do it.

**Three honest costs.**

- **The probe perturbs multithreaded benches.** On a 2t spinning bench the worker keeps spinning through the probe while the main thread stops timing, so the ring drains and the next batch starts from a different queue state. The 1t benches just pause. This is measurable — compare `zcr-with-2t` batch floors with probing on and off — but it's a real interaction and I'd want to check it rather than assume it's negligible.
- **Workload-independence weakens slightly.** During the run the probe shares the box with the bench's own threads, so `env interference` on a 2t bench partly counts the bench. Warmup probes keep the clean version. Worth reporting the two stretches' signals separately if they diverge.
- **Scope.** This is no longer "environment grade from warmup" — the rung's title and the ladder entry would change to something like `feat: environment grade across the run`. Widening -4 seems better than shipping the weak version and replacing it next rung, and it fits the cycle's build-then-demolish order, but it does make -4 the biggest rung of the cycle.

I'd also fold in the per-pair census fix from the last message while touching this code, since the probe loop is being rewritten anyway.

One alternative I'd reject: running probes continuously on a separate pinned thread instead of pausing the bench. It avoids the perturbation but measures a different core than the one under test, which is the wrong core to certify.

The plain version: you were right the first time, and I only applied your idea to the warm-up. If a short box-measurement runs in the same gaps where the batches are already being tallied, the box gets watched for the whole run instead of the first blink of it — and because both measurements then happen at the same moments, we can finally tell whether a wobble came from the machine or from the thing being measured.

aiTitle: Implement and measure high performance SPSC queue

content.text:
Checked the seam: `flush()` does a `select_nth_unstable` over up to 65,536 values plus two full passes plus 65,536 `saturating_record` calls into the histogram. That's roughly 1–2 ms, every 50 ms — the measuring thread is already stopping for ~2–4% of the run at batch boundaries. That number reframes the whole question.

**Grading is already free.** The arithmetic — medians, the split scan, census sums — runs once in `print_report`, after the run is over, over ~120 batch summaries. Microseconds, and none of it during measurement. There is nothing there to offload; a background thread would be moving work that costs nothing off a thread that isn't busy with it.

**The probe can't be offloaded, by construction.** Its job is to measure *this core* at *this instant*. Run it on another CCX and you've certified a different core; run it on another computer and you've certified a different machine. The measurement has to happen where the bench happens — that's what makes it the bench's environment certificate. What it costs is ~256 µs added to a seam that already costs 1–2 ms, so it's a ~15–25% increase in an existing gap, not a new class of cost.

**But your instinct is right — it's aimed at the wrong target.** The expensive thing at the seam is the sort and the 65,536 histogram records, and *that* is what should leave the measuring thread. Hand the filled batch buffer to a consumer thread and let it sort, summarize, and record while the producer fills a second buffer. The seam drops to a pointer swap. The payload is one word — a buffer offset — which is exactly the ffq design, and the project dogfooding the queue it's about to benchmark is a genuinely good look. At 50 ms per batch against ~1–2 ms of work the consumer runs ~30x faster than it needs to, so two buffers never back up. The costs are honest ones: the consumer's cross-core traffic during measurement (trading a gap on the hot core for background L3 pressure), and it wants the ffq to exist first. That's its own cycle, after Todo #2 — not part of -4.

**On opt-in: I'd argue against it as the default posture.** A diagnostic nobody turns on is a diagnostic nobody reads, and the entire point of the env grade is that it's there when someone is puzzling over a histogram they didn't expect. Better to measure the perturbation first — run `zcr-with-2t` with probing on and off and compare batch floors — and let that decide. If it's in the noise, default it on with a `--no-env-probe` escape hatch. If a spinning 2t bench visibly shifts, that's a real finding and worth a flag. I'd rather know than pre-emptively hide it behind an opt-in.

**So, concretely, for -4:** move the probes to the existing batch seams so the env series spans the whole `--duration`, keep the warmup probes as the leading stretch of the same series, shorten each probe to ~128 groups, fix the per-pair census while the loop is being rewritten, and measure the 2t perturbation before choosing the default. Retitle the rung to `feat: environment grade across the run`. The ffq-based seam offload goes on the Todo list pointing at #2, since it needs the queue first.

The plain version: the grading maths is already free — it happens after the run, on a handful of numbers. The thing that actually costs time is the bookkeeping at each block boundary, and that's the piece worth handing to a helper thread later, using the very queue we're about to build. The box-measurement itself has to stay on the core being measured, or it isn't measuring the right thing — but it's small compared to the pause that's already there.

### Warmup was the wrong window

The rung was planned as "environment grade from warmup", and
built that way first. On a quiet 3900X it read A beside a run
grade of A — which prompted the right question, because that
box is known bistable. Three reasons, in ascending order of
how much they matter:

- `calibrate` still runs ~1 s of hard spinning before the
  bench loop (`main.rs`), so by the time warmup probes run the
  governor is already at the top. The grade could not see a
  cold-start ramp because none was left. This one dissolves at
  -6.
- The window was ~17 ms — 16 probes of ~1 ms plus 10,000
  min-now steps. Against governor ramps of tens to hundreds of
  ms that is short.
- Most of all it was the *wrong* window. Grading the first
  17 ms and captioning a 5 s run with the result is this
  cycle's own critique of the calibration grade — certifying
  the room, not the exam — reproduced in miniature.

The fix reuses the batch pipeline's existing shape rather than
inventing one: `flush()` already stops the bench to summarize
a batch, so a probe in that seam costs a fraction of a gap
that exists regardless (the seam already runs a
`select_nth_unstable` over up to 65,536 values plus 65,536
histogram records, ~1-2 ms). Each probe shrank to 128 groups,
~256 µs, since ~120 of them now cover a 5 s run instead of 16
covering its prelude.

The payoff is more than a longer window: every batch now
carries a bench floor and a box floor stamped at the same
instant on the same clock, so movement can be *attributed*.
The first run after the change caught the 3900X mid-shift —
`env step 9.88% @2.138s` beside `run step 9.98% @2.1s`. Same
instant, same magnitude: the box moved and the bench floor
moved with it. An `env` A beside a `run` D would have said the
opposite, that the workload did it. Neither grade can make
that call alone.

### What the probe cannot see

The probe measures the box only while the measuring thread is
running, so time spent descheduled is largely invisible to it
— a ~256 µs probe usually fits inside one scheduling quantum
and is never preempted at all. Measured on the 3900X with the
bench pinned to core 0:

- One spinner `taskset` to the same core: `spread` 0.31% ->
  2.02% (B), `drift` A -> D, `step` A -> D, but
  `interference` only 0.01% -> 0.04%.
- Three spinners on the same core: every signal back to A. Not
  a quieter box — a bench thread that holds its quantum, so
  each probe completes cleanly and the contention lands
  between probes.
- Six unpinned spinners: nothing at all, because with 24 CPUs
  the scheduler left core 0 alone. Affinity does not reserve a
  core, but an idle machine effectively does.

So this grade detects frequency and state movement well and
preemption poorly, and `interference` catches only the rare
large intrusion that happens to land inside a probe. Its
thresholds are set one order of magnitude above the measured
quiet baseline because there is no good upper anchor to
calibrate against; `spread`, `drift` and `step` carry the
detection. We think closing the preemption gap needs a
different instrument — something that reads a counter of
involuntary context switches rather than sampling elapsed
time — which is a separate question from this rung.

### The seam probe's cost, measured

Probing at seams perturbs the bench. Interleaved A/B on the
3900X, `-d 3`, pinned, trimmed mean (`--no-env-probe` off vs
on), five pairs each:

- `zcr-with-2t` (spinning, two threads): 133.18 ns off vs

  warmup stretch. See
  [Grading the box without the bench](#grading-the-box-without-the-bench),
  [Why the probe times groups](#why-the-probe-times-groups),

  [What the probe cannot see](#what-the-probe-cannot-see).

  two grades print

### Warmup was the wrong window

The rung was planned as "environment grade from warmup", and
built that way first. On a quiet 3900X it read A beside a run
grade of A — which prompted the right question, because that
box is known bistable. Three reasons, in ascending order of
how much they matter:

- `calibrate` still runs ~1 s of hard spinning before the
  bench loop (`main.rs`), so by the time warmup probes run the
  governor is already at the top. The grade could not see a
  cold-start ramp because none was left. This one dissolves at
  -6.
- The window was ~17 ms — 16 probes of ~1 ms plus 10,000
  min-now steps. Against governor ramps of tens to hundreds of
  ms that is short.
- Most of all it was the *wrong* window. Grading the first
  17 ms and captioning a 5 s run with the result is this
  cycle's own critique of the calibration grade — certifying
  the room, not the exam — reproduced in miniature.

The fix reuses the batch pipeline's existing shape rather than
inventing one: `flush()` already stops the bench to summarize
a batch, so a probe in that seam costs a fraction of a gap
that exists regardless (the seam already runs a
`select_nth_unstable` over up to 65,536 values plus 65,536
histogram records, ~1-2 ms). Each probe shrank to 128 groups,
~256 µs, since ~120 of them now cover a 5 s run instead of 16
covering its prelude.

The payoff is more than a longer window: every batch now
carries a bench floor and a box floor stamped at the same
instant on the same clock, so movement can be *attributed*.
The first run after the change caught the 3900X mid-shift —
`env step 9.88% @2.138s` beside `run step 9.98% @2.1s`. Same
instant, same magnitude: the box moved and the bench floor
moved with it. An `env` A beside a `run` D would have said the
opposite, that the workload did it. Neither grade can make
that call alone.

### What the probe cannot see

The probe measures the box only while the measuring thread is
running, so time spent descheduled is largely invisible to it
— a ~256 µs probe usually fits inside one scheduling quantum
and is never preempted at all. Measured on the 3900X with the
bench pinned to core 0:

- One spinner `taskset` to the same core: `spread` 0.31% ->
  2.02% (B), `drift` A -> D, `step` A -> D, but
  `interference` only 0.01% -> 0.04%.
- Three spinners on the same core: every signal back to A. Not
  a quieter box — a bench thread that holds its quantum, so
  each probe completes cleanly and the contention lands
  between probes.
- Six unpinned spinners: nothing at all, because with 24 CPUs
  the scheduler left core 0 alone. Affinity does not reserve a
  core, but an idle machine effectively does.

So this grade detects frequency and state movement well and
preemption poorly, and `interference` catches only the rare
large intrusion that happens to land inside a probe. Its
thresholds are set one order of magnitude above the measured
quiet baseline because there is no good upper anchor to
calibrate against; `spread`, `drift` and `step` carry the
detection. We think closing the preemption gap needs a
different instrument — something that reads a counter of
involuntary context switches rather than sampling elapsed
time — which is a separate question from this rung.

### The seam probe's cost, measured

Probing at seams perturbs the bench. Interleaved A/B on the
3900X, `-d 3`, pinned, trimmed mean (`--no-env-probe` off vs
on), five pairs each:

- `zcr-with-2t` (spinning, two threads): 133.18 ns off vs
  134.32 ns on — **+1.14 ns, +0.86%**, and on was slower in
  all five pairs, so it is a bias rather than noise.
- `min-now` (one thread): 22.0 ns off vs 22.1 ns on, at the
  edge of resolution.

We think the difference between the two is the worker thread:
it keeps spinning on an empty ring through the probe, so the
first handoff after the probe starts from a different queue
state. A single-threaded bench just pauses.

Default is **on** anyway. The bias is common-mode in the

without it), and `--no-env-probe` is there for anyone who

3900X's slow state at 24 ns against the others' 22 ns — a 9%
excursion that the flag they were using would have hidden.

### The run grade

Every report ends with a grade (A–F) for *that run*, computed
from its own data. Samples flow through the harness in
time-ordered batches (the header's `batches=N`); each batch keeps
a floor, a mean, and a census count, and the grade reads the
series. Each signal prints its own letter beside its value, and
the composite prints under them on its own line:

```
  run:                 interference 0.02% A, bursts 18% A, drift 9.09% D, step 13.05% @1.0s F
  overall worst case:  F
```

- `interference` — samples that sat above their batch's floor, as
  a fraction of the run. How much other work leaked in.
- `bursts` — batches whose mean sits above the run's median batch.
  Whether that interference was localized in time or spread out.
- `drift` — floor movement from the run's first quarter to its
  last. Did the run finish where it started.
- `step` — the largest floor shift any split of the run divides,
  and when. Catches a shift that drift's endpoints miss — a run
  that moves and moves back reads low on `drift` and high on
  `step`.

**The overall letter is the worst signal, outright.** Each signal
scores 0–4 by counting how many of its four ascending cutoffs it
crosses: below all four is 0 = A, above all four is 4 = F (there
is no E). The composite is the maximum of those scores, so one F
anywhere makes the run F and no number of A's pulls it back —
`step` alone earns the F in the example above. That is why every
signal prints its own letter: the overall letter is always one of
the letters shown on the line above it.

The `environment` letter in the banner works the same way, over
six signals rather than four. Two of those six have no run-side
counterpart, deliberately:

| calibration | run | |
|---|---|---|
| `disturbed` | `interference` | census rate, rebased on the batch's own floor |
| `dirty win` | `bursts` | window becomes batch |
| `drift` | `drift` | floor movement across the measurement |
| `repeat` | `step` | see below |
| `resid` | — | grades a fit |
| `cross` | — | grades a fit |

line) and `cross` (loop-only slope against the dithered two-point
fit) both measure how well a *fit* holds. They exist because
calibration fits a line through a multi-N ladder. A bench run

### The two grades

Every report ends with two grades (A–F), each computed from its
own data: `env` for the **box**, `run` for *that run*. Each
signal prints its own letter beside its value, and each
composite prints under its signals on its own line:

```
  env:                 spread 0.36% A, interference 0.01% A, drift 0.62% A, step 9.88% @2.138s D
  env worst case:      D
  run:                 interference 0.02% A, bursts 18% A, drift 9.09% D, step 13.05% @1.0s F
  run worst case:      F
```

They answer different questions, and reading them together says
more than either alone. `run` describes the numbers above it —
and a run's steadiness is largely its workload's character, so a
blocking round-trip reads worse than a spinning one, correctly.
`env` describes the machine: it comes from micro-probes that time
timer pairs and never touch the bench, so no workload character
enters it. An `env` A beside a `run` D means a bursty workload on
a quiet box; the same letter in both, at the same instant, means
the box moved and took the bench with it — as in the example
above, where both grades caught one state shift ~2.1 s in.

The probes run through warmup and then in the seam at every batch
boundary, so the series covers the whole run on the same time
axis as the batches. `--no-env-probe` limits them to warmup,
which costs the grade its span; it exists because seam probing
perturbs a spinning multi-threaded bench by ~0.9% (measured on
`zcr-with-2t`), a bias that is common-mode in an A/B between two
benches but not in an absolute number.

The `env` signals differ slightly from the run's: `spread` (how
wide a probe's bulk sits above its own floor) replaces `bursts`,
because a bench's spread is mostly its workload while a timer
pair has no character of its own. Note that `env interference`
is the weakest of the four — a probe measures the box only while
the measuring thread is running, so preemption is largely
invisible to it and `spread`/`drift`/`step` carry the detection.

### The run grade's signals

Rung **0.23.0-4 `feat: environment grade across the run`** is built and validated. Cargo cycle clean: `fmt --check`, `clippy --all-targets` (no warnings), 54 tests + 1 ignored, `cargo install` done.

**The change worked, and the first run proved it.** Probes now run through warmup *and* in the seam at every batch flush, sharing the batch series' time axis:

```
  env:   spread 0.36% A, interference 0.01% A, drift 0.62% A, step 9.88% @2.138s D
  run:   interference 0.02% A, bursts 35% B, drift 0.00% A, step 9.98% @2.1s D
```

Same instant, same magnitude — the 3900X's ~9% bistable shift, caught independently by both grades. The box moved and took the bench floor with it. That's attribution, which neither grade could do alone, and it fell out of the shared clock for free. It also retires a Todo that was drafted and dropped for lack of a discriminator.

**The seam is nearly free because it already existed.** `flush()` was already stopping the bench for ~1–2 ms (a `select_nth_unstable` over up to 65,536 values plus 65,536 histogram records). Each probe shrank to ~256 µs since ~120 of them now cover a 5 s run.

**Three measurements that changed decisions:**

- **Perturbation, so the default could be chosen on evidence.** Interleaved A/B, pinned, trimmed mean, five pairs: `zcr-with-2t` reads 133.18 ns off vs 134.32 ns on — **+0.86%, slower in all five pairs**, so a bias not noise. `min-now` was +0.1 ns. We think the difference is the worker thread spinning on an empty ring through the probe. **Default on**, since it's common-mode in the A/B this harness exists for, with `--no-env-probe` as the escape hatch. Two of the five `--no-env-probe` `min-now` runs landed in the box's 24 ns state against the others' 22 ns — a 9% excursion the flag would have hidden.
- **The census fix, and why it mattered more than I predicted.** Counting per pair rather than per group: one 3 µs intrusion is 1 pair in 8,192 (0.012%) but lifts a whole group mean past the cut, reading 1 in 128 (0.78%) — a 64x over-count, alongside the under-count I flagged earlier for intrusions under ~800 ns.
- **A limitation I'd rather you see than not.** The probe measures the box only while the measuring thread runs, so preemption is largely invisible: a 256 µs probe usually fits inside one quantum. With one spinner on the pinned core, `spread` went 0.31%→2.02% and `drift`/`step` A→D, but `interference` only 0.01%→0.04%; with *three* spinners everything read A. So `interference` is the weakest signal, its thresholds are set an order of magnitude above the quiet baseline with no good upper anchor, and the other three carry the detection. Closing that gap needs a different instrument — one that reads involuntary context switches rather than sampling elapsed time — which is a separate question.

**Docs:** chores-05 gained *Warmup was the wrong window*, *What the probe cannot see*, and *The seam probe's cost, measured*; I also reconciled the two subsections written before the redesign rather than leaving them contradicting it. README's "The run grade" became "The two grades" with the new block and the `--no-env-probe` entry.

Not done, deliberately: the ffq-based seam offload (hand the filled buffer to a consumer thread so the ~1–2 ms sort and histogram record leave the measuring thread). That needs the queue from Todo #2 first, and I haven't written the Todo entry for it yet — say the word and I'll add it before the push.

Ready to push when you are.

This pair is the best evidence the cycle has produced. Two things stand out.

**The 3900X validates the attribution.** `env` D (drift 9.89%, step @2.310s) beside `run` F (drift 10.89%, step @2.6s) — and the band table shows the mechanism directly: modes at 21.3–21.8 ns and 24.0 ns, ~10% apart, the two states. The grades say "the box moved", the histogram shows what moving looked like. The ±0.3 s disagreement in step time is expected resolution — two independently-sampled series, each picking a best split with a balance term.

**The 7600x is the headline.** On one invocation: `calibrate` says **environment F** with three WARNINGs ("machine speed changed 11.0% during calibration", "constants differ 12.5% between attempts"), while `env` and `run` both say **A**, every signal 0.00%. They are not contradicting each other — they graded different seconds. Calibration ran during the cold-start frequency ramp and fit its constants across a moving box, so its verdict on *itself* is correct and damning. By the time warmup and the run happened the box was fully ramped, and the run is genuinely pristine: trimmed stdev 0.2 ns over 5 s, two adjacent bands, no tail structure.

That is this cycle's thesis demonstrated on hardware. The calibration grade certified the room while the room was still warming, then warned about an exam that turned out to be flawless. And the `adjusted` column on that run is derived from constants the same banner calls unreliable at 12.5% — which is the argument for -6 in one screenshot.

**A forward problem this exposes, worth recording now.** After -6 deletes `calibrate`, nothing spins for a second before the bench, so the 11% ramp will land inside *our* warmup probes instead. The env series spans warmup plus the run, so on a cold 7600x I'd predict `drift` stays quiet — 16 warmup probes against ~186 run probes, and a first-quarter median of ~50 probes dilutes them — but `step` fires D/F on the warmup-to-run seam, grading the box badly for a run that was clean. The fix is to stop treating the series as homogeneous: the warmup stretch answers "did the box settle before we started" and the run stretch answers "did it stay settled while we measured", and those deserve separate signals rather than one blended `drift`/`step`. That interacts directly with the Dynamic startup warmup Todo, which ends warmup on convergence and would make the first question answerable properly.

I'd like to record both — the two-box comparison as a chores subsection, and the post-`-6` prediction as a note the -6 rung has to deal with — before pushing -4. Want me to write those up and then run `vc-x1 push main`?

content.text:
That's the right shape, and it fixes the blend problem at the root: a warmup ramp isn't a defect, it's the thing warmup exists to absorb. What matters is whether it *finished* before measurement started — and a trailing window that ends in A asks exactly that question.

**The best part is that it collapses two things into one.** Todo #1's convergence criterion and the warmup grade become the same computation. Warm until the trailing window grades A, or until the cap; then the exit condition *is* the letter. Exit on A means the run started post-ramp by construction. Hit the cap and the letter is whatever the trailing window actually scored — which is precisely the "run started unstable" gauge signal that Todo says shouldn't be a silent proceed. No separate K-consecutive-floors-agree tolerance is needed; the signal machinery already written does the job.

**Two definitions it needs.** "Long enough" wants the same shape Todo #1 already uses for pass length — a minimum probe count *or* a minimum wall time, whichever is larger. Count matters because the split detector needs 4 probes a side to say anything; wall time matters because the thing being outrun is a governor ramp measured in milliseconds. And the window's signals should be spread/drift/step; `interference` is the weak one and adds little here.

**One caveat I'd want written down, because it's the failure this can't see.** Steadiness cannot distinguish "settled at the top" from "dwelling at an intermediate P-state" — a staircase dwell is *steady*, so it grades A while being the wrong state. That's the same trap Todo #1's "K defaults to 3" note already identifies, and a trailing window mitigates it only by being longer, not by being different in kind. The honest guard is a minimum absolute warmup time that a lucky quiet window can't short-circuit. I'd resist adding a direction test ("is this the fastest floor seen?") because your own 3900X notes say transitions go both ways, which is why the criterion is agreement rather than direction in the first place.

**The `-v` split is the right call** — and it gives -5 a better observable than it currently has. The full probe table under `-v` (per probe: time, floor, spread, letter) shows the ramp's shape, while the normal report carries one warmup line: letter plus **settle time**. That settle time is a number this project doesn't have yet and it's a genuine machine characteristic — "how long does this box take to become measurable". The settle selftest reading a table of settle times across respawns is far more informative than a table of blended letters.

**On sequencing, one piece is urgent and the rest isn't.** -6 is what creates the problem: deleting `calibrate` removes the incidental ~1 s pre-warm, and the 7600x's 11% ramp moves into our warmup probes. The cheap half of your design — partition the probe series at the run boundary and grade the two stretches separately instead of blending them — is a small change and it makes -6 safe on a cold box. The full sliding-window convergence belongs with Todo #1, which rewrites that phase anyway. So: separate the stretches before -6, land the convergence with #1, and #1's priority is now effectively pinned by -6 rather than by its own rank.

Want me to write this up — the two-box comparison and this design into chores-05, the stretch-separation as an explicit -6 precondition, and the sliding-window/settle-time design onto the Dynamic startup warmup Todo — and then push -4?

The plain version: instead of asking "was the whole warm-up steady", ask "were the last few moments of it steady", and stop warming up as soon as the answer is yes. That single question doubles as both the stop signal and the grade. The trap is that a machine pausing halfway up its speed range looks just as steady as one that has finished climbing, so we still need a minimum warm-up time that a quiet moment can't cut short. And the detailed picture goes behind `-v`, with just a letter and a "settled after N ms" on the normal report.

And the same run's grades: `env step 8.99% @1.003s`, `run step 9.07% @0.4s`. A 9.75% clock climb against a ~9.0% measured step — matching within a percent, with the residual plausibly the part of `min-now` that doesn't scale with core clock. The notes' "We think the 3900X is bistable" can become a measured statement: it dwells at ~4.09 GHz and climbs to ~4.49 GHz once sustained load arrives, dropping back afterward (the tail of the samples shows 3.60 then 1.75 GHz as it decays). Same phenomenon as the 7600x's "machine speed changed 11.0% during calibration".

**And it's the exact trap.** Idle, this box sits *steady* at 87.5% of max. A timing-based steadiness test grades that A and starts measuring — the intermediate-P-state dwell I said no sliding window could catch. One unprivileged file read catches it instantly.

**To answer the register question directly:**

- **x86_64** — `APERF`/`MPERF` (MSRs 0xE8/0xE7): APERF ticks at delivered core frequency, MPERF at the fixed base clock, so their ratio × base = actual frequency. This is what `turbostat` and the kernel's own frequency-invariance code use. Ring 0, so from userspace it needs `/dev/cpu/N/msr` (root) or perf. Max non-turbo lives in `MSR_PLATFORM_INFO`; `CPUID.16h` gives nominal base/max unprivileged on Intel. The TSC deliberately does *not* track current frequency — that's what invariant means.
- **AMD Zen 2+ specifically** — `RDPRU` reads MPERF/APERF from user mode, which would cover both your boxes without root. I'm not certain Linux enables user-mode access to it by default, so that needs verifying by trial rather than assumption.
- **AArch64** — `PMCCNTR_EL0` (core cycles) against `CNTVCT_EL0` (fixed rate) gives the same ratio; ARMv8.4's AMU has a proper APERF/MPERF pair in `AMEVCNTR00/01`. EL0 access is gated by `PMUSERENR_EL0` — Linux exposes the cycle counter via `perf_user_access` on recent kernels.
- **RISC-V** — `cycle` against `time` CSRs, gated by `scounteren`.
- **Max frequency** is generally *not* architectural anywhere — it comes from firmware (MSR on Intel, ACPI/CPPC elsewhere).

**But on Linux you don't need any of that**, which is the practical answer: `cpuinfo_avg_freq` (amd-pstate, APERF/MPERF-derived) or `scaling_cur_freq`, against `cpuinfo_max_freq`, are unprivileged sysfs reads. A read costs microseconds, and the batch seam already costs 1–2 ms.

**What I'd do with it:** carry frequency as a *covariate*, not a grade. Add it to `ProbeSummary` at each seam, and use it in two places. First, the warmup exit condition becomes "at max clock **and** steady" rather than "steady", which kills the dwell trap outright and removes the guesswork from the minimum-time guard. Second, attribution gets a third witness — a step in the run, a step in the env, and a step in the clock is no longer an inference. The report could carry one line: `clock 4.49/4.67 GHz (96%)`.

Two constraints on that: it must stay optional, since `cpuinfo_avg_freq` is amd-pstate-specific and some drivers' `scaling_cur_freq` returns the *requested* rather than delivered frequency, so the tool reads it if present and falls back to timing-only otherwise. And the grade itself should stay a statement about measured time — frequency explains the letter, it shouldn't be the letter.

The plain version: your machine idles at 87.5% of its top speed and jumps to full speed about a second into a run — and that jump is exactly the 9% shift the reports have been flagging. So the mystery is solved. Better still, a file the tool can read for free tells us the speed directly, so instead of guessing "has it stopped changing?" we can just ask "is it at full speed yet?" — which is the one question that timing alone could never answer.

The 7600x is the cleanest result yet, and it closes the loop on the calibration WARNINGs.

```
idle:            4.841 GHz
jumps at +1.0s:  5.440 GHz  → +12.37%
holds:           5440.0xx MHz for the whole 6 s — varying < 0.002%
max:             5.457 GHz  (sustained = 99.7% of it)
```

Calibration on that same invocation reported *"slope estimates differ 12.4%"* and *"constants differ 12.5%"*. The measured clock climb is **12.37%**. Those WARNINGs were reading the ramp, to two significant figures.

**Both boxes do the same thing; only the timing differs.**

| | idle | boost | climb | when it lands | env/run |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3900X | 4.09 GHz (87.5% of max) | 4.44–4.52 | +9.75% | ~1.0 s in — **inside the bench run** | D / D |
| 7600x | 4.84 GHz (88.7% of max) | 5.440 | +12.37% | ~1.0 s in — **inside calibration** | A / A |

So the 3900X isn't "bistable" in a way the 7600x isn't — both idle-dwell at ~88% of max and climb to boost about a second into sustained load. The difference is what that second overlaps. Calibration is ~2x slower on the 3900X (frame/call 52 ns vs 25 ns), so we think its calibration phase runs long enough that the climb spills past it into the measurement, while on the 7600x calibration absorbs the ramp entirely and the bench gets a clock nailed to 5.440 GHz. Same physics, different alignment — and after -6 deletes calibration, neither box gets that absorption for free.

The 3900X also holds its boost less tightly (4.44–4.52, ~1.5% wander) than the 7600x (0.002%), which is a real difference, just a much smaller one than the headline 9%.

**This sharpens the warmup design from last turn.** I said "warm until at max clock and steady" — better is to gate on **clock stability alone**, not a fraction of max. The dwell trap dissolves once you notice the dwell is an *idle* state: warmup is itself sustained load, so the climb happens during warmup if warmup lasts long enough, and on both boxes that's ~1 s. Gating on a percentage of `cpuinfo_max_freq` would need a threshold tuned between 88% and 96% on two AMD desktops — and your thermally-limited Dell would legitimately plateau lower and never reach it. Clock-stable-under-load is directly observable, needs no tuned constant, and handles a laptop that plateaus at 70% because that *is* its honest sustained clock. Report the ratio for information; don't gate on it.

That's the portability question the covariate design hinges on. It's also the most interesting box of the three for a different reason: a thermally-limited laptop should show the *opposite* shape, starting fast and decaying under sustained load, which would exercise env `drift` in the direction neither desktop can produce.

content.text:
You were right to push, and it changes two of my numbers.

**The "idle at 88% of max" figure was my own measurement artifact.** Reading `cpuinfo_avg_freq` wakes the core it's reporting on, and APERF/MPERF only accumulate in C0 — so polling at 4 Hz or 20 Hz held cpu0 at ~4.09 GHz, and that's what I reported as idle. A single cold read after 6 s quiet, with the reader pinned off cpu0, gives **3.588 GHz**. Genuinely quiet, the box sits at **1.746 GHz** — `lowest_nonlinear_freq` exactly, which is the 1745645 that showed up in the decay tail I'd glossed over. Floor is 563 MHz. So the quiet-to-sustained span is 1.75 → 4.49 GHz, a factor of 2.6, not 9%.

**And the ramp is fast.** At 50 ms resolution the climb runs 4.07 → 4.54 GHz in about 150–200 ms, then holds 4.49 ± 1.5%. It starts the moment calibration pins core 0 and starts hammering it — roughly 1.3 s after launch, which is process startup plus the `systemd-inhibit` re-exec.

**So "already blazing" is exactly right, for the current build.** Calibration runs ~1 s of sustained load on core 0 before any bench warmup, and the clock reaches boost within the first fifth of that. By the time warmup's first probe runs, the box has been at 4.49 GHz for the better part of a second. That's the pre-warm I identified as accidental — and now I can say how accidental: the ramp is ~200 ms and calibration covers it five times over.

**Which leaves the 9% steps needing a better explanation than I gave.** In the first experiment the clock transition and the measured step genuinely coincided (9.75% vs 8.99%). In this one the transition completed before warmup and the run graded A on every signal, with only the env stretch showing 4.4% — and that run's calibration also read `disturbed 2.79% C`, because my 20 Hz polling loop was itself load. So the honest statement is narrower than my last message: the clock moves ~9–12% between light-load and sustained-load states on both boxes, and *when that transition lands inside the measurement window* both grades see a step of matching size — but whether it lands inside depends on the box's recent load history, not on a fixed schedule. That is the duty-cycle dependence the notes already describe, now with a mechanism attached rather than a mystery.

What survives intact from the last two turns: the 7600x's calibration WARNINGs measure the clock ramp to two significant figures (12.4% reported vs 12.37% measured); frequency is readable unprivileged on both boxes; and the post-`-6` risk is now *worse* than I framed it, because deleting calibration removes a pre-warm that covers the ramp five times over, so warmup will see the whole 200 ms climb from wherever process startup leaves the clock.

I'd like to write up what's solid and explicitly flag what isn't. Specifically: the frequency mechanism and the 7600x WARNING correspondence as measured findings, the observer effect as a caveat on any future frequency reading the tool does itself (it would be reading the core it's running on, which is the good case — but it must never poll another core and call that idle), the stretch-separation as a -6 precondition, and the clock-stability warmup design on Todo #1 marked as design-not-yet-measured. ### The clock behind the anomaly

The 3900X's "bistable" ~9% shift and the 7600x's calibration

run `amd-pstate-epp`, which exposes delivered frequency
through unprivileged sysfs

measured rather than inferred.

**Measured, 2026-07-28.** Sampling `cpu0`'s frequency while a
pinned `min-now` ran:

- **3900X** — clock climbed to 4.44-4.52 GHz under sustained
  load against a 4.674 GHz max. In the run where the
  transition landed inside the measurement window, the climb

  independently-measured steps, agreeing within a percent.
- **7600x** — climbed to 5.440 GHz against a 5.457 GHz max,

  seconds. The same invocation's calibration reported
  "independent slope estimates differ **12.4%**" and
  "constants differ **12.5%** between attempts". The
  calibration WARNINGs were reading the clock ramp to two
  significant figures.
- **Ramp shape** — at 50 ms resolution the climb takes
  ~150-200 ms, beginning when calibration pins core 0 and
  starts hammering it, roughly 1.3 s after launch (process
  startup plus the `systemd-inhibit` re-exec).

**What this does not say.** Whether the transition lands
inside a measurement window depends on the box's recent load
history, not on a schedule: a later 3900X run had the climb
complete before warmup and graded `run` A on every signal. So
the mechanism is established; its *timing* remains
duty-cycle-dependent, which is the behaviour the earlier notes
described without a cause.

**A correction, and a caveat for any future reader.** An
earlier draft of this section reported both boxes "idling" at
~88% of max. That was an artifact of the measurement:
APERF/MPERF only accumulate in C0, so reading a core's
frequency wakes it, and polling at 4-20 Hz held the observed
core at ~4.09 GHz. A single cold read after 6 s quiet, taken
from a reader pinned to another core, gives 3.588 GHz, and a
genuinely quiet 3900X sits at 1.746 GHz — exactly

quiet-to-sustained span is therefore a factor of 2.6, not 9%.

The lesson generalizes to any frequency reading this tool
might take: reading the core it is *already running on* is the
sound case, because that core is in C0 by construction.
Polling some other core and calling the result idle is not a
measurement.

### The clock as a warmup criterion (design, unmeasured)

The obvious use is the warmup exit condition, and it solves a
problem no timing-based criterion can. A steadiness test
cannot distinguish "settled at the top" from "dwelling at an
intermediate P-state", because a dwell is *steady*. A clock
reading distinguishes them directly.

We think the right gate is **clock stability under load**, not
a fraction of max:

- A threshold on `cpuinfo_max_freq` would need tuning between
  the two boxes' sustained fractions (96.1% on the 3900X,
  99.7% on the 7600x) against their pre-load readings, and a
  thermally-limited laptop would plateau lower still and never
  reach it — while that plateau *is* its honest sustained
  clock.
- Stability under load needs no tuned constant. Warmup is
  itself sustained load, so the climb happens during warmup if
  warmup lasts long enough; the ~200 ms measured here is the
  scale.
- Report the ratio for information; do not grade on it. The
  letter should stay a statement about measured time, with the
  clock explaining it.

Portability caveat: `cpuinfo_avg_freq` is amd-pstate-specific,
and some drivers' `scaling_cur_freq` returns the requested
rather than the delivered frequency. Any use must be optional
— read it where present, fall back to timing-only otherwise.
An Intel laptop is the next box to check, and the interesting
one: a thermally-limited machine should show the opposite
shape, starting fast and decaying under sustained load, which
is the direction neither desktop can produce.

- **7600x** — climbed to 5.440 GHz against a 5.457 GHz max,
  **+12.37%**, and then held to within 0.002% for six
  seconds. The same invocation's calibration reported
  "independent slope estimates differ **12.4%**" and
  "constants differ **12.5%** between attempts". The
  calibration WARNINGs were reading the clock ramp to two
  significant figures.

  ~150-200 ms, beginning when calibration pins core 0 and
  starts hammering it, roughly 1.3 s after launch (process
  startup plus the `systemd-inhibit` re-exec).

**What this does not say.** Whether the transition lands
inside a measurement window depends on the box's recent load
history, not on a schedule: a later 3900X run had the climb
complete before warmup and graded `run` A on every signal. So
the mechanism is established; its *timing* remains
duty-cycle-dependent, which is the behaviour the earlier notes
described without a cause.

**A correction, and a caveat for any future reader.** An
earlier draft of this section reported both boxes "idling" at
~88% of max. That was an artifact of the measurement:
APERF/MPERF only accumulate in C0, so reading a core's
frequency wakes it, and polling at 4-20 Hz held the observed
core at ~4.09 GHz. A single cold read after 6 s quiet, taken
from a reader pinned to another core, gives 3.588 GHz, and a
genuinely quiet 3900X sits at 1.746 GHz — exactly
`amd_pstate_lowest_nonlinear_freq`, and the value that appears
in the decay tail after a run ends. The floor is 563 MHz. The
quiet-to-sustained span is therefore a factor of 2.6, not 9%.

The lesson generalizes to any frequency reading this tool
might take: reading the core it is *already running on* is the
sound case, because that core is in C0 by construction.
Polling some other core and calling the result idle is not a
measurement.

### The clock as a warmup criterion (design, unmeasured)

The obvious use is the warmup exit condition, and it solves a
problem no timing-based criterion can. A steadiness test
cannot distinguish "settled at the top" from "dwelling at an
intermediate P-state", because a dwell is *steady*. A clock
reading distinguishes them directly.

We think the right gate is **clock stability under load**, not
a fraction of max:

- A threshold on `cpuinfo_max_freq` would need tuning between
  the two boxes' sustained fractions (96.1% on the 3900X,
  99.7% on the 7600x) against their pre-load readings, and a
  thermally-limited laptop would plateau lower still and never
  reach it — while that plateau *is* its honest sustained
  clock.
- Stability under load needs no tuned constant. Warmup is
  itself sustained load, so the climb happens during warmup if
  warmup lasts long enough; the ~200 ms measured here is the
  scale.
- Report the ratio for information; do not grade on it. The
  letter should stay a statement about measured time, with the
  clock explaining it.

Portability caveat: `cpuinfo_avg_freq` is amd-pstate-specific,
and some drivers' `scaling_cur_freq` returns the requested
rather than the delivered frequency. Any use must be optional
— read it where present, fall back to timing-only otherwise.
An Intel laptop is the next box to check, and the interesting
one: a thermally-limited machine should show the opposite
shape, starting fast and decaying under sustained load, which
is the direction neither desktop can produce.

   bench for ~1-2 ms (a `select_nth_unstable` over up to

   - the payload is one word, a buffer offset — the exact

     queue it benchmarks
   - double-buffered: at ~1-2 ms of work per 50 ms batch the
     consumer runs ~30x faster than it needs to, so two
     buffers never back up
   - honest cost: the consumer's cross-core traffic runs
     *during* measurement, trading a gap on the hot core for
     background L3 pressure. Measure it the way the -4 seam
     probe was measured (interleaved A/B, pinned, trimmed
     mean) rather than assuming
   - blocked on the ring existing — see the

     `ffq-spsc-notes` bookmark rather than `main`
